item.title: What an economics Nobel Prize winner knows about pricing
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News
What an economics Nobel Prize winner knows about pricing NPR's Ailsa Chang chats with Michael Woodford of Columbia University, who was one of two Americans awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics. AILSA CHANG, HOST: All right. Two Americans have just been awarded the Nobel Prize in economics. Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University are being honored for their work on how to bring stability to cycles of economic boom and bust. But they base their macroeconomic models off of their microeconomic research into how people actually decide to buy stuff and how businesses actually decide to price that stuff. Economist Michael Woodford is with us now. Welcome, and congratulations on winning the Nobel Prize. I don't get to say that every day on the show (laughter) . MICHAEL WOODFORD: (Laughter) I don't get to hear it every day, either. Thanks a lot. CHANG: So what were your first thoughts when you found out you got the Nobel Prize? WOODFORD: Well, I wasn't terribly awake, I'm afraid (laughter). I was trying to sleep when they called. CHANG: Of course. WOODFORD: Yeah. Because it's six hours later in Stockholm. CHANG: Yeah. From the East Coast. Yeah. WOODFORD: And my wife said I didn't sound very enthusiastic about it... CHANG: (Laughter). WOODFORD: ...But I mean, it was because I was... CHANG: Groggy. WOODFORD: ...At best, half awake. (LAUGHTER) CHANG: Well, I want to better understand your work, and I'm going to try to keep up as best I can, at least on the basic concepts. So part of your research was on how businesses set prices, right? And I want to use a very concrete example. Like, let's say you're a trucking company, and you're thinking about adjusting your rates because the cost of diesel fuel unexpectedly surges. How would your work apply to that example? WOODFORD: Well, a thing that is particularly central to my work is stressing the extent to which decisions that people make often are forward-looking, are not just a response to immediate conditions... CHANG: Yeah. WOODFORD: ...But have to also take into account where you think things are headed. In the case of changes in costs that people have some reason to think is probably very temporary, I think, often, prices don't respond, that something that you think is likely to be lasting is going to be more likely to encourage people, more quickly, to already price it into the prices they're charging. So this issue of the extent to which people are able to make good guesses about where things are headed is something that the work that I've done particularly stresses. CHANG: OK. Let me give you another concrete example. WOODFORD: Sure. CHANG: So, like, yesterday, the president of the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank said that she heard from a business owner who's planning to raise prices more than his costs have gone up because he just expects those costs to keep climbing. How concerning is that, when businesses start to anticipate higher costs and raise their own prices in response maybe disproportionately? WOODFORD: Well, I think that illustrates that it isn't just the current costs... WOODFORD: ...That are going to matter for that decision. It matters a lot what people think about where they could be going, you know, their guesses, their fears. And that's one reason why my work has stressed the idea that policymakers should be concerned about trying to give people reassurances about, you know - not false reassurances - but if they themselves intend not to let certain things happen or to make them not very likely to happen, that being able to communicate that to the public so that their expectations about where things can go are, in fact, not significantly out of line with what really happened, that actually is important for the economy. CHANG: If I could just jump in 'cause you're talking... WOODFORD: Yeah. CHANG: ...About something very important. You have stressed in your work that policymakers should make an effort to communicate clearly and accurately and in... WOODFORD: Right. CHANG: ...Proportion so that families and businesses can plan accordingly. How do you think Congress or President Trump or the Federal Reserve are doing on that front, on their communication skills? What do you think? WOODFORD: Well, of course, it's a challenging thing. You know, I don't... WOODFORD: ...Want to imply that I could just communicate much better than them. And, you know - but often policymakers don't think as much as they should about how important this is to their role. I think that, often, they take the view that it's enough to react to whatever is happening once it happens. You should think about the fact that your behavior being predictable actually has big benefits for the economy, and that people can see that this fits into a pattern of behavior that they can count on. CHANG: So in this time where people are quite focused on affordability, what advice do you have for people out there feeling just unsettled and unsure about the state of the economy right now? Any words of assurance or warning (laughter)? WOODFORD: Well, I certainly understand why it's an issue. I mean, it's not that economists should tell people to calm down. I think that it's appropriate for the government to indicate that it's keeping its eye on this issue, and to use monetary policy - make it clear that there is a commitment to keeping an eye on prices. I think it is - to some extent, it's a failure of public policy to not have kept a better lid on things. CHANG: Michael Woodford, cowinner of the Nobel Prize in economics. Thank you, and congratulations again, Professor Woodford. WOODFORD: Thanks. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. item.title: Family of Franklin High student who fell to his death calls for security, accountability
item.description:
Source: LA Times
No ‘back to normal’ at Franklin High as campus grapples with trauma after student’s death - Family members of Xavier Nungaray-Martinez, 17, who died after falling from a fourth-floor corridor at Franklin High, challenged the medical examiner’s finding of death by suicide. - Relatives believe bullying is a problem at the school. - At a protest outside the school board meeting, family members called for campus police and stronger security. The Franklin High School community — its students, teachers and parents — are struggling to find a way forward as they mourn the death of senior Xavier Nungaray-Martinez, who was repeatedly hit by another student and then fell over a fourth-story railing on campus, a traumatic sequence of events that has sundered any sense of normalcy and prompted districtwide demands for safer schools. Students and others have gathered for at least three evening vigils near a sprawling makeshift memorial at the Los Angeles Unified School District campus in Highland Park. The campus has gone on lockdown twice in two weeks amid threats — none substantiated. But the emergency drills and parent notifications further jolted fears on campus, which includes a middle school in addition to the high school Xavier attended. “The mood has been really solemn,” said Mark Ramos, who teaches history and ethnic studies at Franklin High. “A lot of students are having a hard time processing all of this.” Teachers and students report attendance is down. Some teachers have slowed the pace of their classes to give students space to grieve. “It’s a lot more different now,” said sophomore Kimberly Peralta, 15, after school last week. “We just all hope he rests in peace.” Los Angeles police and school officials met with parents last week but have released little publicly. The Los Angeles Police Department said Oct. 7 they are investigating allegations that “bullying may have contributed to the student’s death,” but have yet to announce whether there is a connection. The county medical examiner’s office determined that Xavier died by suicide and toxicology reports are pending. Despite the several shocking videos that show a portion of the confrontation when Xavier was being hit and then his death, there are many unanswered questions as to exactly what happened. The videos don’t capture the entire sequence of events and it’s unclear what precipitated the fight. On Tuesday, Xavier’s father and two other family members challenged the medical examiner’s determination. They do not believe Xavier used drugs and had never heard him talk about drugs on campus. “He was not suicidal,” said his father, William Amaya, speaking publicly for the first time since his son’s death. “So just to put that out there, because they’re saying that he was, but he was not.” Xavier’s father recalled the 17-year-old as a kind, shy teenager who enjoyed gaming and was looking forward to graduation. “He was looking forward to start working,” Amaya said. “He had plans. He was trying to move on.” Amaya was among a group of about half a dozen parents — including two other family members — who demonstrated outside Tuesday’s Board of Education meeting. “We’re trying to get our voices heard,” said Stephanie Amaya, who is William Amaya’s cousin. “Xavier has started a movement for all of us, and we’re here to just ask for protection for our kids. Bring back the school police. That’s our main priority, and we want justice. That’s why we’re here outside, waiting for them to hear us.” She vowed to continue the protests as long as necessary. Last week, a group of district parents called for officers to be returned to campuses, reigniting a long-simmering debate about police patrols at Los Angeles Unified schools. Other Franklin parents have focused on counseling efforts and have not supported a police presence. In 2020, under pressure from community and student activists who called for defunding police, the district board voted 4-3 to remove officers from campus and slash funding for the school police by 35%. A much smaller police force continues to conduct patrols and respond to emergencies. “We need every single school and every single kid to have a chance and feel protected in their school,” said Stephanie Amaya, who has started a petition calling for increased surveillance measures, on-campus police officers, training for non-police security staff, improvements to internal campus communication and, especially at Franklin High, the installment of safer railing systems. Family members said they believe Xavier was bullied and see it as a significant problem at Franklin High. School board member Rocio Rivas, who represents the area and whose child attends Franklin High, described a campus working through “a lot of pain and confusion” in a social media post last week. She did not respond to requests for an interview. Franklin Principal Marine Davtyan did not respond to an interview request. District Supt. Andrés Chait in a board meeting praised school staff who “came together” to support students and pledged that the district will give Franklin “whatever you need.” Video taken moments before his fall shows Xavier on the floor of a classroom being struck at least six times by a male classmate. No video has emerged that shows what happened before the encounter. Video also shows a teacher standing between the students as Xavier gets slowly to his feet. The other student strikes one more blow from behind, knocking Xavier to the ground. He stumbles up and runs from the classroom. Another video, taken seconds later, shows Xavier at the railing. A male student who appears to be the other person involved in the conflict is approaching Xavier when Xavier vaults over the railing. Police have not released information about the person seen on the video striking Xavier. Xavier’s aunt, Elizabeth Amaya, said Tuesday she believes that if not for the fight, Xavier would not have fled the classroom. Elizabeth Amaya also has a daughter at the school, a senior, who also feels that bullying is an issue on campus. Xavier’s family members stressed that providing police officers should not come at the expense of counseling, which also needs to be increased or improved, they said. William Amaya added that he is a graduate of Franklin High and that there used to be one or more officers on campus who broke up fights and deterred others by their presence. Former school board member David Tokofsky said Franklin High used to have two assigned officers out of concern for keeping the campus safe from the influence of a local gang. Ramos, the Franklin teacher and elected chair of the North Area for United Teachers Los Angeles, said he’s not convinced fighting and bullying are worse at Franklin High than at other campuses, but he said the school does need more resources. Franklin students have had, even before the tragedy, a comparatively high level of mental health needs, according to Ramos. For the moment, the school is flooded with counselors, but Ramos said typically there is only one psychological social worker for more than 1,000 students. “That’s frankly not enough,” Ramos said, who recalled there being two such workers a year or two ago. “It’s a matter of where the district puts their priorities.” Three Franklin High mothers told The Times there has been an increase in fights this year on campus. The district declined to answers questions about the frequency of fights at Franklin and did not say if staff had been cut at the high school. “As with all LAUSD schools, District staffing allocation procedures were followed,” a statement said. Lockdowns since Xavier’s death have exacerbated tensions. Last Thursday, the campus locked down following reports that a student had a gun. Police investigated but did not find a weapon. A day later, the school received “an anonymous call threatening our campus,” according to a message the school principal shared with parents. “After investigating, L.A. School Police determined that our campus remains safe for instruction and that the report was not credible,” the message said. Vanessa Alvarez, whose children attend Franklin High, said calls from the school about fights and medical emergencies are nearly weekly, an uptick from what she received in prior years. Alvarez attended a meeting last Thursday between senior district officials and Franklin parents to share her concerns over safety, but ultimately left feeling that families were not given a concrete plan by the district. “More than anything, I wanted to know about safety, but there weren’t any responses,” Alvarez said. Ramos, the veteran teacher, predicted the unease on campus will continue. “I don’t think there’s going to be a back to normal for a while,” Ramos said.

item.title: Inflation sizzled in September — and Social Security benefits will get a boost
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Business
Inflation sizzled in September â and Social Security benefits will get a boost Nights are getting colder, but inflation is heating up. A report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed consumer prices in September were up 3.7% from a year ago. That's a larger annual increase than the previous month. A spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran drove the cost of living higher. Prices jumped 0.6% between August and September. "It's not looking good," said economist Brian Bethune of Boston College. "The main problem, of course, that everybody knows is gasoline prices. But also heating oil." Heating oil is a close cousin of diesel fuel. The cost of the fuel oil has jumped 74% in the last year, which is hard on families in New England who rely on heating oil to stay warm. Stripping out volatile energy and food prices, what's known as "core inflation" was 2.6% in September. That's also a bigger annual increase than was tallied in August. The artificial intelligence boom has raised the cost of memory chips, affecting all sorts of consumer electronics. Apple, for example, raised the price of older-model iPhones last month by $100 apiece. Social Security recipients will get a raise Shortly after the inflation report was released, the Social Security Administration announced that benefits will increase by 3.6% next year. The annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices in July, August and September. The jump in benefits amounts to an extra $75 a month for the average Social Security recipient. Advocates for seniors welcomed the increase. "It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, healthcare and other everyday expenses," said AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan. Loading... But critics complain that the cost-of-living adjustment doesn't reflect seniors' actual expenses, which often include higher costs for healthcare. "It won't be enough for most seniors to even tread water financially," said Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare. Treading water would be an improvement for most workers, whose paychecks are not keeping pace with today's rising prices. Prices are climbing faster than paychecks Average wages in September rose just 3%, so the typical worker's buying power has eroded over the last year. "People are kind of saying, 'Something isn't right with that,'" Bethune said. "I'm working harder. I'm more productive. And this is not a square deal." Inflation is not nearly as high as it was in 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. But every time prices start to level off, the economy is rattled by a new supply shock, such as President Trump's double-digit tariffs or the war with Iran. Beth Hammack, who heads the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank, worries the cumulative effect of these shocks could make inflation more entrenched. Hammack told a group of economists this week about a Cleveland-area retailer she'd heard from who is raising prices not just to cover today's costs but the higher costs that may come in the future. "This could be a sign that an inflationary mindset is taking hold," Hammack said. "When people expect higher prices, they make decisions with this in mind. It can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that makes it harder for monetary policy to bring inflation back down." Policymakers at the Federal Reserve will weigh the new inflation data when they meet in two weeks to discuss interest rates. Investors now see about a 50-50 chance the Fed will raise its benchmark rate in October in an effort to combat inflation. An earlier version of this story said that inflation was higher in 2002, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The invasion and the resulting spike in prices were in 2022.

item.title: 2 Americans win Nobel Prize in economics for work on boom-bust cycles
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Business
2 Americans win Nobel Prize in economics for work on boom-bust cycles Last Nobel prize of the year to be announced for economics Two Americans have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on how to smooth boom-and-bust cycles to limit inflation and unemployment. Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University were honored for their focus on how individual households and businesses make decisions on purchases and pricing — work that became the foundation of the "New Keynesian" approach to economics. The importance of that work has been underscored in recent years by the pandemic, which pushed millions of people out of work, and the supply shocks that followed, driving up the cost of living. "Regardless of the causes, an important goal for governments and central banks is to reduce the amplitude of these swings and limit the risk that the economy gets stuck in a situation with high unemployment or loses control over inflation," said John Hassler, the chairman of the economic prize committee. This award is not one of the original five, but a "memorial" prize that honors Alfred Nobel.
After the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes persuaded policymakers that government sometimes needed to stimulate demand during downturns to curb unemployment, or tamp down demand during boom times to limit inflation. "This is the Keynesian recipe, and it worked well until it didn't," said Tim Boppart, a member of the prize committee. In the 1970s, the economy was hit by rising unemployment and inflation simultaneously. "The Keynesian recipe was shattered," Boppart says. Hall and Woodford added some necessary ingredients, focusing on the individual households and businesses that help shape the larger economy. Hall concentrated on demand and how households make purchasing decisions, guided not only by current purchasing power but what they expect their incomes will be in the future. "If consumers see dark clouds on the horizon, they cut back on consumption already today," Boppart says. Woodford focused on the supply side and how businesses set prices. Here again, expectations are key. Historically, it was costly to change prices, so businesses try to think ahead and set prices that would cover costs for an extended period. Because both households and businesses are forward-looking, the Nobel laureates argued, policymakers should communicate their plans clearly to the public. "One of the themes in my work is that government authorities shouldn't view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy, independent of what people in the economy understand," Woodford told reporters after the prize was announced. Woodford says tools intended to smooth out boom-and-bust cycles work better when people know what the government is trying to accomplish, and he urged policymakers to talk directly to the public about "why the things that are being done are being done."

item.title: OpenAI says employee caught planting listening device
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said Tuesday one of its employees was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was found in one of its San Francisco offices. A 35-year-old Saudi national working as an engineer was arrested on Friday, a week after the device was discovered in a conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco. After the device was discovered, the company reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee. A federal investigation is ongoing. The suspect, who appeared in court on Tuesday, has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. The criminal complaint did not specify what the suspect might have wanted to do with the recordings. It did add, however, that the suspect used a tool to inquire about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars. How was the device found? OpenAI said the device was discovered a few days after it was allegedly planted by the suspect. "We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," a spokesperson for the artificial intelligence company told the Associated Press. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the spokesperson added. According to the US Justice Department, the suspect wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and hid it inside a television located in an "executive conference room." He was seen on camera near the room several times despite not having authorization to sit in meetings there. After this was noticed, another camera was installed in the room that captured the suspect on film checking on the stashed device. item.title: The liver transplant system tried to fix its sex bias. Did it work?
item.description:
Source: Vox
In theory, getting a donor liver in the United States when you need one should be an extremely equitable process: The sickest patients with the greatest chance to benefit from a donated organ should jump to the front of the line regardless of their gender, race, or other factors. The liver transplant system tried to fix its sex bias. Did it work? The algorithm that ranks candidates just got an update, and the results are in. But in practice, things look quite different. One study from 2020 showed that women were 8.6 percent more likely than men to die waiting for a liver transplant and 14.4 percent less likely to receive a deceased donor liver transplant compared to men. That gap may not seem enormous, but it still represents a significant disparity. As it turns out, it’s rooted in the very system that’s supposed to make the process fairer, a process that unintentionally ranks women lower on the waitlist for livers. The system in question is known as the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD). The scoring model has been used since 2002 to rank candidates on the waiting list based on how likely they are to survive without a liver transplant in the short term. The higher your score, the reasoning goes, the sicker you are and the more urgently you need a liver transplant. One of the values used to calculate the score is creatinine — a waste product made by muscles as they break down proteins or other compounds to release energy. In medicine, the creatinine levels in your blood are used to determine how well your kidneys are functioning because they process and remove creatinine. And this is where the system designed for equity gets a little less than equitable for some patients. Creatinine levels are affected by muscle mass, and women typically have lower muscle mass than men. A man and woman experiencing the same level of kidney dysfunction will therefore have different levels of creatinine in the body. The MELD model doesn’t take this difference into account — and so lower levels of creatinine in a woman’s blood can make her seem healthier than she is, bumping her farther down the liver waiting list. In 2023, Dr. Ray Kim, a transplant hepatologist at Mayo Clinic in Arizona who developed the original system, debuted a new model called MELD 3.0. The model not only seeks to address the sex disparity in liver access but also improve the accuracy of scores for all patients. Among other changes, it takes into account the sex of the transplant candidate and uses it to adjust the MELD score by 1.33 points for women. This is meant to address the difference in creatinine levels between men and women and provide a more accurate understanding of how sick a female patient really is. Simple fix, right? Even though MELD 3.0 took the sex disparity in liver access seriously and developed changes to combat it, early research on its efficacy found that even this new and improved system hasn’t yet brought men and women to parity on the liver waitlist. And the problem may lie less with what MELD 3.0 did than with what it did not do, prompting the question: Are we focusing on the wrong problem? Before the MELD score, liver transplants were largely conducted on a first-come, first-served basis. Those who were added to the waiting list first, received livers first. If a really sick candidate was added to the waiting list late, say because of delayed diagnosis, they would almost certainly die while waiting for a liver to become available. The original MELD fixed that problem by creating a measure of urgency that was easy to calculate. The initial model used three main blood test values — bilirubin, creatinine, and a measure of blood clotting time — and later improvements also took into account the sodium level. - Women are more likely than men to die waiting for a liver transplant in part because the system used to rank candidates on the liver waiting list underestimates how sick women are. - In 2023, the liver transplant system adopted a new version of that scoring model, which adds 1.33 points to women’s scores to correct for differences in muscle mass between the sexes. Early research shows that the new model increased transplant rates for women, but the gains were transient. - Experts say that the score is only part of the problem. A donated liver has to physically fit inside the body receiving it, so smaller candidates end up waiting longer for a liver they can accept. - The organ allocation system currently has no way to prioritize smaller livers toward smaller patients, who are more often women. Fixing this is likely the key to ensuring equitable liver access for men and women. Traditionally, the MELD model assigns a score between 6 and 40 to liver transplant candidates. MELD 3.0 adds 1.33 points to women’s scores to account for the differences in creatinine levels between the sexes. The new model also measures albumin, an additional biomarker, and adjusts for interactions between the different variables. Sommer Gentry, a professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and contributor to the paper on MELD 3.0, said that using sophisticated algorithms with more biomarkers not only helps to better predict risk for women, but using a more accurate model also benefits the whole population. The researchers estimate that this fine-tuned MELD 3.0 model will reduce at least 20 waiting list deaths per year. Last year, around 800 liver transplant candidates died while waiting for a liver. But creatinine is only one of the two main problems that create a disparity in liver access for women. The second, Gentry says, is body size, an issue that’s not addressed by MELD 3.0. A transplanted liver has to physically fit inside the body of a recipient, and women are typically smaller than men, so a very large liver cannot be offered to a small woman. But the reverse is not necessarily true because receiving a liver that is small for the potential recipient doesn’t typically harm the candidate. “The smaller you are, the less likely you are to be offered something that’s actually going to work for you,” Gentry said, adding that women end up waiting longer to receive a liver that will actually fit their body. Part of the conversation on sex disparity in liver access is based around which of the two problems — creatinine or body-size interventions — to fix first, and whether it is possible to create equity by addressing just one of the two, Gentry said. MELD 3.0 was an attempt to remove the former barrier. “I think that some other papers are coming out that suggest that perhaps the other aspect of size matching is still a concern and still possibly not addressed by the resulting liver transplant system,” Gentry said. Why is the new model still falling short? Gentry believes that MELD 3.0 has increased liver transplant rates for female candidates since its adoption in 2023. But early research, however, suggests that the new model falls short of fixing the problem. Studies done on MELD 3.0’s impact on liver transplant rates for women indicate that the model increased the number of liver transplants for female candidates — but the gains were short-lived. An analysis published in July of nearly 10 million daily records from over 60,000 candidates on the US liver transplant registry found that rates of completed liver transplants for women increased in the period immediately after MELD 3.0 was implemented, but the increase was temporary. Women’s estimated odds of receiving a transplant drifted back to pre-MELD 3.0 levels by the end of the study period, 15 months after the new model was implemented. Women on the waiting list and women who had received a transplant also had higher scores in the three months right after MELD 3.0 took effect, but their scores later fell back to levels comparable to those of men. Both the successes and shortfalls of MELD 3.0 demonstrate how rethinking existing policies and standards can help reduce inequities in organ access and healthcare. The authors think that the early surge in liver transplant rates for women was a onetime catchup. MELD 3.0 pushed a group of women who had been stuck on the list — sicker than their old scores suggested — over the priority threshold all at once, leading them to receive liver transplants. Notably, the one effect that did persist was that under MELD 3.0, women received more “organ offers” than before. Every time a deceased donor liver becomes available, the system generates a ranked list of the patients suitable to receive that organ. Under MELD 3.0, the number of times an available liver was offered to a female candidate increased, probably because their (more accurate) MELD 3.0 scores better reflected how sick they were. But they’re not necessarily receiving those livers, presumably because of organ size issues. These findings suggest that revising the MELD criteria alone may not be enough to eliminate the sex disparity, especially if the body-size disadvantage is part of the problem. The authors say that a patient’s sex is merely a poor proxy for the real issue — we don’t have allocation systems in place to ensure that candidates with smaller body sizes also have the same robust access to livers. If we could figure out how to better address questions of body size in organ donation, the benefits could be enormous. According to Gentry, body-size disparity affects the organ allocation system in general. Similar issues arise with heart and lung transplants too, where the size of the organ relative to body size has to be taken into consideration during organ allocation. She says that a size-aware organ allocation system would therefore benefit patients on the waiting list across the board. Whether an available organ is the right fit for the potential recipient should be weighed heavily in allocation algorithms, rather than just a list of ranked waitlisted candidates. “That should be a larger consideration in sorting the patients who will be offered a certain organ — to ask if this organ is especially suited to one kind of patient over another,” Gentry said. Under such a system, she said, smaller livers could be offered first to the smallest candidates on a ranked list of those who are also sickest. The assumption is that a smaller candidate will have to wait longer for a viable liver that fits them, even if they have a very high MELD score. For such a policy to be instituted, the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network – a nonprofit that oversees the distribution of donor organs — would have to approve it. And before such a system could be presented to the regulatory organization, more research is required. It is often the case in medicine that our definition of what counts as a healthy body is measured against the average white male. This too often lowers access and quality of care for both women and people of other races. For example, the standards for creatinine levels in blood reduced access to kidney transplants for Black transplant candidates for years until recent efforts were made to start correcting it. In that sense, both the successes and shortfalls of MELD 3.0 demonstrate how rethinking existing policies and standards can help reduce inequities in organ access and healthcare. The conversations and critiques that followed its rollout have exposed a clear gap in organ allocation strategies, one that disadvantages a large group of patients. Closing that gap, not just in liver transplantation but across the board, could bring us a step closer to equity while also making more efficient use of the organs available to save lives. “There’s no mechanism right now, if a small liver is available, for offering it preferentially to the small women who might not be able to accept lots of other organs that are becoming available,” Gentry said. While fixing the model to rank women more accurately on the liver waiting list is a start, including body-size considerations in the organ allocation system might be the real bottleneck to address.

item.title: Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News
Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life. Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on. "James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'" Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words. "I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice." Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University. On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers. On how playing piano connects to her grief I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ... I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity. Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. … What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life. He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting. Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people. I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer. Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

item.title: How will a diesel deal with Russia impact the U.S. market?
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World
How will a diesel deal with Russia impact the U.S. market? The price of diesel hit an all-time high in the U.S. in September. Can President Trump's deal for Russia to release more diesel onto the market bring the price down? AILSA CHANG, HOST: OK, there are plenty of legal and political questions surrounding President Trump's deal to get Russia to release more oil to the U.S. and global markets. And, of course, a lot of Americans are wondering how that deal could affect the price of diesel. NPR energy reporter Willa Rubin joins us now to talk about all of this. Hi, Willa. WILLA RUBIN, BYLINE: Hi, Ailsa. CHANG: Hi. OK, so give us the lay of the land here. What is happening with the price of diesel in the U.S. right now? RUBIN: Well, it hit an all-time high a few weeks ago, which is important for the U.S. economy. You know, our industrial supply chain relies on diesel, tractors that farmers use, trucks that bring your food from farms eventually to the grocery store. If diesel is expensive, that contributes to the price of everything that you buy. Now, the price of a gallon has come down a little bit since that September high. On average, it's now $6.27, according to AAA, but that is still really high. Diesel is about $2.60 more than this time last year. CHANG: OK, and explain this to me. What did President Trump say about how he expects this deal would work exactly? RUBIN: Yeah, so in a post on Truth Social on Friday, President Trump said that Russia had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and to global markets immediately. But, like, is that a little or a lot in terms of how much the U.S. actually uses? CHANG: Yeah, which is it? RUBIN: Yeah. So to put this in context for the rest of October, Will O'Neil is an analyst at S&P Global Energy. He's a follower of all things diesel. WILL O'NEIL: Because I could even do some quick Excel math. So 300,000 tons over the course of 20 days is... RUBIN: I love that you broke out an Excel spreadsheet mid conversation (laughter). O'NEIL: That's what I do. That's my job. RUBIN: So he figured out that if you convert tons to barrels and the U.S. uses up to 4 million barrels a day, the entire amount expected to be released in October adds up to about half the diesel the U.S. uses in just one day. O'NEIL: It's drops in the bucket. RUBIN: Drops in the bucket. And if you do some more math using the entire amount expected to be released over the coming months, O'Neil said it adds up to about nine days' worth. CHANG: Let me ask you this. Is Russia really in any position to export all of this diesel? RUBIN: Analysts in the U.S. don't know, but what... CHANG: OK. RUBIN: ...They do know is that Russia's refinery capacity has been significantly reduced by Ukraine's strikes. O'Neil says it's probably reduced 40- to 45% of their capacity. O'NEIL: Ukrainian drone strikes have taken so much of its refining capacity offline that it just simply doesn't have the diesel production to send to global markets. RUBIN: He says this deal does not change that reality. Russia has had an export ban since July, though they partially lifted it on Saturday. Also worth noting, the U.S. has had wide ranging sanctions on Russian energy since its full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. On Friday, the Treasury Department announced it was temporarily waiving sanctions on diesel for about six months. And this has gotten some pushback from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle. This is a really complicated situation, Ailsa, with a lot of moving parts. CHANG: Clearly. OK, if Russia really can bring this diesel to market, could that help lower prices in the U.S., you think, eventually? RUBIN: Big picture, what drives diesel prices is global demand. And there's a global diesel deficit right now. A good chunk of that is due to the war in Iran. Claudio Galimberti is a partner and chief economist at Rystad Energy. He says the world is missing up to 1.5 million barrels per day that normally come from the Middle East and another million barrels that would come from Russia. CLAUDIO GALIMBERTI: So it's a huge gap, and this deal only address (ph) a very small portion of that. CHANG: OK, Willa, I'm no economist, but it sounds like he doesn't think this will really lower prices all that much. Am I getting that right? RUBIN: Yeah. Analysts told me we will only start to see big meaningful drops in prices by solving these bottlenecks by ending the wars. CHANG: That is NPR's Willa Rubin. Thank you so much, Willa. RUBIN: Thank you so much, Ailsa. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. item.title: How NATO plans to combat potential attacks on the alliance from Russia
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World
How NATO plans to combat potential attacks on the alliance from Russia NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with former U.S. Assistant Secretary for European Affairs Dan Hamilton about NATO's detailed plans to counter any possible Russian attack on the alliance. STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: Dan Hamilton has been listening with us. He served as deputy assistant secretary for European affairs at the State Department in the 1990s. He was responsible for NATO security issues. Welcome to the program. DAN HAMILTON: Good morning. INSKEEP: Why is NATO needing to talk about its defense strategy against a Russian attack now? HAMILTON: I think that the - as Teri just said, you know, the allies in Europe are uneasy. They're uneasy about the continued U.S. commitment to the alliance. They're nervous about Russia's not only conventional war against Ukraine, but the uptick in these unconventional assaults all across the rest of Europe. You know, the U.S. B-1 bombers had to relocate back to the U.S. from the U.K. because of a suspected assault on a U.K. base. There is sabotage at Leipzig Airport in Germany. There's been arson attacks, cyberattacks. So they wanted to hear directly that NATO has a strategy and that NATO, you know, has got it, as General Grynkewich said at the Warsaw Forum. INSKEEP: Would you talk me through that threat? I mean, when you mentioned the British airbase, of course, that's something that British authorities blame on Iran, not Russia, but some of the others could be traced to Russia. Is there a way for Russia to seriously attack and gain ground in Europe without the full-scale ground offensive that didn't work very well for them in Ukraine? HAMILTON: Well, the - it's hard to see Russia launching some full-scale attack, especially if it's bogged down right now in Ukraine and any mass movement of forces, of course, would be detected early by NATO. But, you know, think about what Russia's goals might be, is to demoralize European governments, distract them from attention to Ukraine or that they question their own policies to supply Ukraine with armaments that they might then need and get European publics to question their own government support for Ukraine. You know, the Leipzig attack in Germany is - was in a German state right next to crucial state elections in East Germany, where the far right gained significantly, just a couple of weeks ago, and they all have a pro-Russian attitude there. So instead of thinking of assault, think of a small scenario. You know, you could have armed individuals without insignia just crossing a river in a Baltic state like Narva, Estonia, which is right on the Russian border. Would NATO go to war because of something like that? Is there a consensus among allies on how you respond? These kinds of scenarios are what keep NATO officials up at night because it might be a political move by Putin sometimes to split the alliance rather than... INSKEEP: Yeah. HAMILTON: ...A conventional assault. INSKEEP: When you talked about armed men without - armed troops without insignia crossing a border, of course, that's the way Russia seized Crimea once upon a time. HAMILTON: That's right, in 2014. INSKEEP: Does the United States in some way undermine the alliance by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, something that clearly dismays Europeans? HAMILTON: Well, they're just at cross-purposes, you know, for the president to announce this, even though there is a U.S. law, as a bipartisan group of U.S. senators said, to stop - that prevents U.S. dollars from financing Putin's war. He went ahead with that announcement anyway. At the same time, as Teri mentioned, the EU yesterday launched the biggest batch of sanctions against Russia that it has since the 2022 invasion. So we are definitely working at cross-purposes here. INSKEEP: Does it surprise you that the sanctions have not ultimately brought Russia down? Their economy was hurt for a while but seems to have gradually recovered. HAMILTON: It's a wartime economy. It's being propped up by Chinese support, and I don't think it can sustain itself if it keeps going like this. So the sanctions do hurt, and they force Putin to make tough choices. INSKEEP: Dan Hamilton is a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Institute of Johns Hopkins University. Thanks very much for your time. HAMILTON: Thank you. item.title: DNA and vehicle-tracking help French investigators recover stolen Renoirs
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World
DNA and vehicle-tracking help French investigators recover stolen Renoirs NANTERRE, France — DNA left on a protective painting cover helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover what they suspected were preparations for another art heist, a French prosecutor said Monday. Four men were given preliminary charges in the investigation into the Sept. 8 theft from the small Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera. The charges include organized theft and criminal association, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said. One painting, "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano," suffered a tear. The other, "Young Woman at the Well," had slight damage to its frame, Bessone said. He estimated their combined value at 4.2 million euros ($4.7 million). The thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence, entered the museum through the ground floor and cut clips securing the frames of four paintings. An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that "apparently caused the perpetrators to panic," Bessone said. "As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve," he said. The DNA found on the abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old already under investigation in a drug trafficking case in which police were tracking his vehicle, Bessone said. Vehicle-tracking data showed that the suspect, accompanied by a 41-year-old man, went to the home of a third man shortly after the theft, Bessone said. Police surveillance also showed that the 29-year-old on Oct. 3 visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — home to a large modern art collection. The suspect then met with a fourth man known to police from art theft and forgery cases in 2001 and 2003. Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the "very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent." The two men suspected of carrying out the museum theft have been given preliminary charges of "theft committed by an organized gang" and "criminal association," among other counts. They were sent to prison pending further investigation. The have denied wrongdoing, Bessone said. The third suspect acknowledged receiving the paintings at his home and hiding them behind a wall built beneath a staircase after the theft. Investigators recovered the Renoirs from the hiding place, Bessone said. The fourth suspect acknowledged seeing photographs of the paintings but said he did not immediately recognize them. Both of those suspects were given preliminary charges of "concealment" of stolen paintings. They were released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving France. Two additional people who had been arrested were released without charge. The theft renews concerns about museum security The Renoir Museum occupies the final home of the leading French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who lived there until his death in 1919. It is the best-known attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a Mediterranean coastal town between Cannes and Nice. The theft revived painful memories of the spectacular theft of crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and renewed calls for better security and funding at the many cultural sites across France. Christian Sainte, national director of judicial police, said Monday that the country "is repeatedly targeted by organized criminal groups that carry out theft operations targeting valuable objects that are part of our cultural heritage" in museums, castles, places of worship, private homes and art galleries. French museums recorded 23 cases in 2025 and about 10 this year, he said.

item.title: Many Iranians who go to Turkey to find jobs are exploited
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World
Many Iranians who go to Turkey to find jobs are exploited Desperate Iranians are finding work in Turkey to make ends meet, but many are being exploited and left with nothing but more debt. AILSA CHANG, HOST: What if you could make a year's worth of pay in just a couple months? I mean, there is a catch. You would have to leave your family behind. That's a choice that many Iranians make. With a worsening economy, some decide to travel to Turkey, hoping to find temporary work to provide for their families. But the jobs that they're looking for don't always materialize. NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi was there when a bus full of Iranians pulled up in Istanbul. (SOUNDBITE OF BUS HORN HONKING) HADEEL AL-SHALCHI, BYLINE: It's about 6:30 in the morning. A bus that says Royal Iranian Travel just pulled up, and more than a dozen people just walked out of the bus. A lot of them look very, very tired. (SOUNDBITE OF SUITCASE HITTING THE GROUND) AL-SHALCHI: Forty-five-year-old construction worker Abbas pulls his suitcase from the bus and waits on the sidewalk of the Aksaray neighborhood in Istanbul. This place has been a hub for Iranian tourists and businesspeople for decades. Today, it's dark and cold. People light up cigarettes and huddle in small groups. ABBAS: (Non-English language spoken). AL-SHALCHI: Abbas traveled for days from the city of Qom to Turkey, hoping to find work and send money back to his wife and two kids. AL-SHALCHI: "Our economic situation isn't good at all," says Abbas. ABBAS: Very bad. Very bad. AL-SHALCHI: Iran's inflation rate hovers at 90%, and the cost of living has skyrocketed since the war began. Today in Iran, the price of meat has gone up over 40%. Bread has tripled. All the Iranians who spoke to NPR for this report are working illegally in Turkey and asked us not to use their full names for fear of deportation. Many will travel days to find work under the table here on a 90-day tourist visa. Abbas got in touch with an agent who matches Iranians looking for work with jobs. AL-SHALCHI: "I was told the employer is supposed to come pick me up," he says, rubbing his hands in the cold. But Abbas says he doesn't have a phone number for the employer or the agent. He just trusts that someone will come get him. RAMIN: (Non-English language spoken). AL-SHALCHI: "No, you can't trust the agent," says 34-year-old Ramin (ph), as he stands in front of a closed bank. He has a friend who secured him a job and a place to stay. AL-SHALCHI: "If you don't know the employer, they mess with you," he says. "They don't pay you. They throw you out." It's what happened to 24-year-old Yasin. (SOUNDBITE OF SUITCASE WHEELS ROLLING) AL-SHALCHI: Every day, he rolls his suitcase down a cobblestone street from the park where he sleeps to the mosque where he waits with a handful of other homeless Iranians looking for work. YASIN: (Through interpreter) When this mosque opens, we can use the bathroom and drink some water. AL-SHALCHI: Yasin wears a sweatshirt with the hood pulled around his face to keep out the cold. YASIN: (Through interpreter) Even if you find work in Iran, you only make enough for that night's dinner. AL-SHALCHI: Yasin left his family in central Iran and traveled six days by land to get here. He paid an agent a hundred dollars to find him work at a doorknob factory. YASIN: (Through interpreter) The agent takes it all at once. There's no guarantee that the employer will pay. None of it is clear. AL-SHALCHI: Yasin was kicked out of the factory after working there for a month, with only a quarter of the pay he was promised. YASIN: (Through interpreter) I haven't saved even a few cents. AL-SHALCHI: And now, Yasin only has a couple of days left on his visa. YASIN: (Through interpreter) I'm scared the police will catch me and deport me. I don't have the money to go back to Iran. MOHAMED REZA: (Non-English language spoken). AL-SHALCHI: Travel agent Mohamed Reza reads off a list of names taped to his desk - Iranians who, like Yasin, didn't have the fare to go home. REZA: (Non-English language spoken). AL-SHALCHI: "Since I have a bus company, I send them back for free," he says. "I keep a record of the names, but I don't expect them to repay." Reza says it's been hard to sell bus tickets to Iran lately, but the other way is different. AL-SHALCHI: "Buses come from Iran nearly full of workers who have lots of hope," he says. UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Non-English language spoken). AL-SHALCHI: Back at the mosque, 35-year-old Rasul hangs out with other Iranians looking for jobs. For almost 15 years, he's come to Turkey for months at a time to work. RASUL: (Non-English language spoken). AL-SHALCHI: "With a year of work in Iran, I couldn't put together the kind of money I make here in two months," he says. But after the war, the market in Turkey is now saturated with job-seeking Iranians. He hasn't been able to find work for weeks. He missed his son's first day of school. AL-SHALCHI: "I gave up on the money and just want to leave," he says. It's hard for him to go back having lost money traveling to Turkey. AL-SHALCHI: "This time, it's become like hell for me," he says. "It's like death." Hadeel Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.

item.title: Both Russia and Ukraine are using AI-powered drones on the battlefield
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World
Both Russia and Ukraine are using AI-powered drones on the battlefield A Ukrainian company that got rich making smartphone-controlled cameras to watch pets at home now outfits first-person-view drones with an image recognition system powered by artificial intelligence. AILSA CHANG, HOST: Both Russia and Ukraine are already using drones powered by artificial intelligence on the battlefield. It's part of a high tech arms race that has many people worried, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He's warned that AI could start leading decisions on the battlefield as early as next year. Meanwhile, the founder of one of Ukraine's top companies producing AI-powered drones says that they're helping Ukraine survive a war waged by a much larger enemy. NPR's Joanna Kakissis reports from Kyiv. JOANNA KAKISSIS, BYLINE: It's a good microphone. YAROSLAV AZHNYUK: It's almost like a weapon. KAKISSIS: We meet Yaroslav Azhnyuk in a conference room, and for security reasons, he asked us not to reveal much else about the location. He's 37, a computer scientist and serial entrepreneur who spent years in Silicon Valley. Before the war, he was known for cofounding a successful company called Petcube... (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) KAKISSIS: ...Which makes smartphone powered cameras that watch and even entertain your pets. AZHNYUK: These cameras allow pet parents to watch their pets when they're not at home and fling treats to them and shine a laser toy for them. KAKISSIS: Then, in 2022, Russia launched its full scale invasion of Ukraine, and Azhnyuk, like many Ukrainian tech leaders, turned his focus to the defense space. AZHNYUK: I was like, OK, I got to move on from my role as a CEO of Petcube and do something to protect my country. And so now we're making not cameras that fling treats, but cameras that fling explosives to people who came to occupy our land. KAKISSIS: The cameras he's talking about are part of an image recognition system incorporated into first person view, or FPV, drones. AZHNYUK: This year alone, Ukraine will produce over 7 million of FPV drones, those small drones. They've fully transformed the battlefield, and they have become, for our era, what the tank or machine gun have become for World War I. KAKISSIS: Azhnyuk runs the defense tech firms The Fourth Law and Odd Systems. AZHNYUK: We are the leaders in autonomous drones and thermal cameras. We're No. 1 in Ukraine, maybe to some extent, close to the top globally. KAKISSIS: Team has developed a widely used strike drone called the Lupynis-10-TFL-1. It combines a small affordable FPV drone with an autonomous terminal guidance system. That means the drone has an onboard computer and AI technology that takes control during the final phase of the flight. AZHNYUK: But it's very different from, say, the kind of AI that sits on those data centers that power Claude or even kind of AI that does self-driving for your Tesla. KAKISSIS: Azhnyuk says the AI technology in his company's drones uses simple tools to recognize images and make smart software. AZHNYUK: Which then allows you either to navigate autonomously without a human or to choose a target autonomously or to fly towards the target autonomously. KAKISSIS: Dozens of Ukrainian military units already use The Fourth Law's autonomous drone, which is named after the 20th century Ukrainian poet Anatoliy Lupynis. He endured decades of Soviet imprisonment and torture. The Fourth Law has named all of its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians in the last century. AZHNYUK: It is important for us to help to resurrect those people. They're still with us. Their ideas are still with us, and they are now fighting back. (SOUNDBITE OF DRONE BUZZING) KAKISSIS: The company's teams test the drones every day. We meet one team in an overgrown field outside Kyiv. They've set up a foldout table near a copse of trees and a hornet's nest. Nice to meet you, too. Very nice to meet you. STAB: No worries. KAKISSIS: A slight, sandy-haired man greets us. STAB: I'm head of the test and integration team, so our main duties is integration of our autonomous system on the different kind of drones. KAKISSIS: He uses the military call sign STAB (ph). The company asked NPR not to reveal this location or the identities of those who work here for security reasons. STAB points to a drone. STAB: So you see here is our camera plus microcomputer inside. KAKISSIS: Oh, there it is. Oh, there it is. STAB: And all of the mind is here. KAKISSIS: The microcomputer inside the drone runs on a deep learning neural network that's been fed hours of combat footage. That's how it recognizes targets. STAB: What target is like vehicle, light armored vehicle, tank and flying object, et cetera. KAKISSIS: The drone begins its flight guided by a pilot. He also asked us to use his call sign, PROFESSOR (ph). The pilot is the one who selects the target. He guides the drone with a control stick. PROFESSOR checks a video monitor. There's a red flash. OK, is it locking there? STAB: Yeah, it's locked, and if you see, the system is working by itself. KAKISSIS: The drone has locked onto the target. (SOUNDBITE OF CAR ENGINE) KAKISSIS: A dilapidated car that a company employee is driving along a dirt road. PROFESSOR puts down the control stick, and the drone flies itself to the car. The microcomputer inside constantly runs algorithms to keep it on course. KAKISSIS: STAB says AI drones are useful because they're hard to jam, and he insists there are safeguards in place so the drones don't go rogue. AZHNYUK: It's very obvious for the public to be concerned. KAKISSIS: Back at the conference room, Yaroslav Azhnyuk says it's obvious the public is concerned about the dangers of AI. AZHNYUK: You know, any kind of tool can be used for good or for bad, and it's - in the end, it's the human that decides how to use that tool. KAKISSIS: And he says his company's AI-powered drones are not autonomous killer robots. AZHNYUK: They're very far from a terminator of kind of scenario, right? These are just sort of calculators. Like, they're no more likely for a terminator uprising than a warehouse with artillery shells. KAKISSIS: He does, however, acknowledge that AI warfare is developing quickly. AZHNYUK: It's not unthinkable to imagine that some years in the future, there will be drones that will be able to make their own decisions about designating something as a target or not. KAKISSIS: And Ukraine must keep up, he says, because Russia is also using AI-powered drones to attack. AZHNYUK: So if we're not able to react just as fast, we have lost. And obviously, after we've lost, there is no way for us to argue about the ethics of AI. KAKISSIS: The most important thing, he says, is don't die. Joanna Kakissis, NPR News, Kyiv.
