item.title: Actor Selma Blair removed from plane by police after altercation
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Culture
Actor Selma Blair removed from plane by police after altercation Actor Selma Blair was taken into custody after a flight from Los Angeles to New York for being physically abusive and injuring two flight attendants, authorities said Monday. Police took Blair, 54, into custody late Sunday night when the Delta Air Lines plane was parked at the gate at New York's John F. Kennedy Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement. There was no immediate response to a request for comment from the airline. Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to a hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority said. The FBI, which is responsible for investigating all assaults aboard aircraft, declined to release details. "Yesterday, we were informed by our partners at Port Authority Police Department of a potential assault aboard a flight that arrived into JFK. As per long-standing DOJ policy, we do not comment on ongoing investigations," said Sydney Kleinmann, a spokesman for the FBI NY. Messages seeking comment were not immediately returned by the state and federal prosecutors' offices in New York. A message left with Blair's publicist seeking comment was not immediately answered. In a statement to several media outlets, a Blair representative said she had a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Blair had major roles in films including 1999's "Cruel Intentions," 2001's "Legally Blonde" and 2004's "Hellboy." In recent years she has been an advocate for disability rights. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018. In 2023, she joined President Joe Biden at the White House to celebrate the anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act. In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she regretted on a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles, saying that she mixed alcohol with medication, which made her black out.

item.title: Older Americans are struggling with food affordability
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Economy
Older Americans are struggling with food affordability High food prices are pushing some older adults to make difficult budget decisions when it comes to what's available to eat. That can mean scaling back on produce in favor of cheaper, processed foods and relying more on food pantries SCOTT DETROW, HOST: Going to the grocery store has gotten a lot more expensive in recent years. Ground beef, tomatoes and coffee have all seen big spikes. Those higher prices can be especially hard on older adults on fixed incomes. Nicole Grundmeier with the Midwest Newsroom and Harvest Public Media has been out speaking with seniors. NICOLE GRUNDMEIER, BYLINE: Once a month, the people who live in this low-income retirement community in Storm Lake, Iowa, gather to create their own food pantry. They divide and distribute donations from the Food Bank of Iowa. UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: How many of the peppers? UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Two. GRUNDMEIER: Today, fresh pineapples, potatoes and bell peppers pile up on tables. The residents can go through and take the items they need. Linda Rufus, who is 67, relies on this pop-up pantry. LINDA RUFUS: Well, I'm thinking about how I'm going to rob Peter to pay Paul because food prices are extremely high, and I have to really weigh out what's more important or how I can get the most out of a meal. GRUNDMEIER: Rufus says she's stretching every dollar and trying to find cheaper, more filling food items. While she loves beef, she's now buying ground turkey. Her neighbor, Toni Keller, is also shopping at the pop-up pantry today. The 65-year-old spent years outside the workforce as a caregiver, which reduced her retirement benefits. TONI KELLER: I get a whopping $304 a month 'cause I had a sick child, so most of my time was spent with her. GRUNDMEIER: That Social Security payment isn't nearly enough to cover Keller's living expenses, including food. She relies on the federal food assistance program SNAP and other help, like this pop-up pantry. She recently completed treatment for breast cancer and tries to prioritize eating fresh fruits and vegetables. KELLER: After having cancer, you're eating a little differently, which costs more money to do. GRUNDMEIER: Nationwide, food prices were 3% higher this June compared to the same time last year, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. That follows larger spikes during the COVID-19 pandemic. High food prices are pushing older adults to make difficult budget decisions which could affect their health. Jessica Johnston is a senior strategist at the National Council on Aging. JESSICA JOHNSTON: So much of the conversation around SNAP and food insecurity really has been around children and families. And older adults really are often a forgotten population. GRUNDMEIER: In 2024, an estimated 7.7 million Americans ages 60 and up experienced food insecurity or a lack of adequate food at some point, according to the USDA's Economic Research Service. That's about 1 in 10 older Americans. Gina Plata-Nino is the director of policy and advocacy at the Food Research & Action Center. She says Social Security benefits don't protect older adults from hunger. GINA PLATA-NINO: Your rent didn't decrease because you turned 60. Your utilities didn't decrease because you turned 60. Neither did fuel, and neither did food. GRUNDMEIER: And nearly half of older adults who carry credit card debt are using their cards to buy food, according to a 2025 survey by the AARP, the advocacy group for people 50 and older. Back in Iowa, Linda Rufus says she and her fellow residents at the Storm Lake Senior Housing are grateful for the pop-up pantry. RUFUS: Because if it were not for the food banks, you know, supplying us with food, you know, we would be in a lot worse condition than we are. GRUNDMEIER: Even so, experts say seniors on fixed incomes will likely continue to feel the squeeze of high food costs. For NPR News, I'm Nicole Grundmeier in Des Moines, Iowa. (SOUNDBITE OF BADBADNOTGOOD AND GHOSTFACE KILLAH SONG, "STREET KNOWLEDGE (FEAT. TREE)")

item.title: Sauna research gathers steam
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Health
Leading researchers in heat exposure are coming together to reach a consensus on what we know — and don't — about the health benefits of sauna and its potential for treating and preventing disease. AILSA CHANG, HOST: Modern life offers us a lot of control over temperature. We push the thermostat up or down, put on layers, take them off. We avoid extreme temperatures when we can help it. But some scientists believe that putting people in a hot spot in a controlled way could be good for them. NPR's Will Stone recently traveled to Norway to speak with researchers who are interested in sauna and other forms of heat. WILL STONE, BYLINE: The study of how heat affects our body isn't new. In the late 1700s, a British doctor ran a bold set of experiments. He brought steak and eggs into a piping-hot room and observed that, unlike the food, his own body did not cook. Our acute response to heat and how our body keeps cool is now well understood. Faced with extreme temperatures, blood vessels dilate, heart rate speeds up, and blood is pushed to the skin where it cools down as we sweat. Our body releases hormones and activates heat shock proteins that protect our cells. This knowledge has shaped medical care, for example, with heat-related illness. But how to use heat to improve health... HANS HAGGLUND: Unfortunately, that question is easy to answer. There is not very much evidence out there. STONE: Dr. Hans Hagglund is a hematologist at the Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm, though he was here in Norway, where I interviewed him in a sauna for a symposium on heat therapy. (SOUNDBITE OF SAUNA STEAM) STONE: He even wrote a popular book on the topic, earning him a title from the Swedish Sauna Academy. HAGGLUND: After that, I was named the Sauna Doctor. STONE: Hagglund is thrilled the practice is attracting more followers. It's become a social outlet and a staple of the broader wellness movement. HAGGLUND: It's really booming, and it's here to stay, I think. STONE: Meanwhile, most of the claims floating around online are not based on the kind of well-controlled human studies that medicine relies on to establish the benefits and risks of a given therapy. This is what Hagglund and others are hoping to change. EARRIC LEE: Give it prominence. Let people understand that, you know, this is not some woo-woo or, you know, some kind of snake oil. STONE: Earric Lee is a postdoctoral researcher at the Montreal Heart Institute and lead scientist at a nonprofit called the Sauna Research Foundation. And he spends a lot of time explaining to friends and other scientists what he does. LEE: When I tell them heat therapy, they're like, heat therapy - what do you mean heat therapy? I'm like, well, you use heat to improve your health. Is that a thing? STONE: It is, and Lee's pushing for the field to gain more legitimacy. That's why his organization recently convened scientists from around the world at a trendy sauna resort outside Oslo so they could hash out how to rigorously study heat therapy and to form an organizing scientific body to steer the field. Ultimately, the goal is to answer some pretty basic questions. What's it good for? How hot should it be? What are the risks? LEE: How much do I do and all that kind of stuff. And I have a hard time answering that question, and I know listen to your body doesn't cut it. People want information. STONE: There are certainly reasons to believe heat, delivered as a strong stimulus in a time-limited manner, holds promise for health. It works our cardiovascular system similar to light exercise and delivers some of the same benefits. Plus, influential research, mostly from Finland, suggests people who spend more time in the sauna live longer and have lower rates of cardiovascular disease and even Alzheimer's. While these findings are encouraging, Lee says they are observational studies, so you can only conclude so much about safety or how effective it is. LEE: To change policy, we have to do the not-so-sexy stuff. We need to test it out in a trial. STONE: All of this could lay the foundation for medical societies or governments to one day recommend heat therapy alongside other lifestyle interventions, like exercise. And the research is starting to pick up. For example, Lee has run one of the only randomized controlled trials on sauna bathing, showing that adding it to exercise offered extra benefits for people at risk of cardiovascular disease. Others are focusing on mental health. In her research, Ashley Mason, a clinical psychologist at the University of California, San Francisco, is looking at different forms of heat therapy - infrared machines, Finnish sauna and heated blankets. ASHLEY MASON: Scientists around the world are getting interested in this and figuring out ways to study heat therapies, but we're all over the place. We need to establish - how do we write about our work? What are the standards? What are the norms? What are the terms? What are the definitions? Do we agree about them? STONE: These are the growing pains for a new field of scientific study, even one built on age-old practices. Will Stone, NPR News, Oslo. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

item.title: MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
item.description:
Source: BBC News
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said. Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases. At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders". He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones. He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons. However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years. Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly". Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks. "With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak," he said. "So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding." He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand." His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine. Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved". He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute". He added that he was "worried" about the ongoing debate on Russian interference. "I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters. Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK. The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities. Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites". Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique". He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK." The incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police. Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard". The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response." Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia. On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual. "We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with AI-enabled drones adding a new twist." Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes". "These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on." Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are". He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities". In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely. Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism. He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent." Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK". He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

item.title: Missiles intercepted near Riyadh after Saudi coalition hits Yemen fuel depot
item.description:
Source: BBC News
A missile launched by Yemen's Houthi movement hit a building owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran overnight, after a Saudi-led coalition struck a fuel depot near the Yemeni capital, Sanaa. The Saudi energy ministry said the Houthi attack caused a "limited fire" in an administrative building at Aramco's headquarters complex. Saudi authorities reported that several missiles and drones were intercepted elsewhere, and that falling debris injured four people in the capital, Riyadh. The Houthis said they targeted Aramco and Riyadh's airport in response to the coalition's strike on the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday. The Iran-backed group also warned that there would be further attacks in the coming days. International Monetary Fund director Kristalina Georgieva said the escalating conflict could have "potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere". The Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, vowed on Tuesday that the Houthis would "bear the consequences" of their recent attacks on the kingdom, including a missile strike on Riyadh's airport on Saturday that killed 13 people. The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa. The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive against the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other front lines. On Tuesday evening, coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said its forces intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards Dhahran, but that debris fell in a residential area. Later, the Saudi energy ministry said an Aramco building in the city was targeted, causing a "limited fire" but no injuries. Sources with knowledge of the incident told Reuters news agency that a ballistic missile hit an office tower in the company's headquarters complex, causing extensive damage and a fire that spread between the sixth and 10th floors. "[The] top three floors have gone," one Aramco employee was quoted as saying by AFP news agency. Maliki said the coalition also intercepted missiles and drones launched towards Riyadh, al-Kharj and Haradh, as well as the country's south on Tuesday and Wednesday morning. The General Directorate of Civil Defence said two women, a man and a child were injured by debris from two intercepted cruise missiles in Riyadh, which also caused "limited material damage" to 15 homes in the city. The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said on Wednesday morning that they had targeted Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, an Aramco refinery in Riyadh and the capital's King Khalid International Airport with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. "Operations towards Saudi depths will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities," he added. The Houthis had threatened a "harsh and painful" response to the Saudi-led air strikes in Yemen on Tuesday afternoon. Houthi-run media reported that the air strikes targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha Central Station, on the western outskirts of Sanaa, as well as its facilities at the Ras Isa oil terminal on the Red Sea coast, north of the port city of Hudaydah. Two civilians were killed and two others were injured in the Ras Isa attack, the Houthi-run health ministry said. The coalition had earlier issued a rare warning to civilians to evacuate the al-Sabaha fuel depot, saying it was planning a "special operation". Queues reportedly formed at petrol stations in Sanaa following the warning, with many residents worried about shortages. The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products". The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner". Maliki said the coalition targeted al-Sabaha and other facilities because they were supporting Houthi "terrorist military operations". "The militia has used these sites in their entirety to support its war effort by supplying its arsenal of missiles and [drones], which threaten the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the safety of airports, ports, and commercial vessels in the Red Sea," he added. Houthi-run media also reported on Wednesday that a Saudi air strike in the south-western district of Shamayatayn killed a woman and that artillery fire killed two civilians in the north-western district of Shadaa, near the Saudi border. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran. US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly... and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices". Speaking to reporters, he did not answer a question on whether he had made a decision to help the Saudis retaliate against them, but said he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene. Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes. Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children. More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.

item.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
item.description:
Source: BBC News
Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday. The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said. Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury. "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC. The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning. "Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement. "We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added. In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks." The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said. The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied. OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism. The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said.

item.title: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
item.description:
Source: BBC News
A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners". Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people had been killed and 21 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. He said "several energy facilities" in Kyiv had been hit without giving more detail. Kyiv has reported multiple Russian strikes since US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine two days ago. In the early hours of Wednesday, Klitschko said the "massive missile attacks" had knocked out power to parts of Kyiv. Kyiv officials have urged residents to stay in shelters after declaring a red alert due to a "missile threat". Following the strikes on Tuesday, Zelensky said: "Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people. "This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added. "It is important that the world does not stay silent about this. And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing." It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and comes as Zelensky prepares to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv. Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats. Earlier on Tuesday, Trump denied that was the case. "We are helping them and we are sharing intel," he said. "We want the war to end. So we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end." Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before." But he demurred when asked if Russia had broken a ceasefire. He said both countries want the war to "come to an end" but "just don't know how to get there". It comes after Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow his country to hold presidential elections, following comments from Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president". Following Trump's announcement on Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Lavrov added that under any ceasefire, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war. CHPP-4, which provides heating and electricity to the Dniprovskyi district and parts of the Darnytskyi district, has been hit multiple times during the war. It was severely damaged in a separate Russian missile attack in February this year, which forced it to shut down. That strike left more than 1,000 residential buildings without heating and hot water, along with 47 schools, 72 kindergartens and 18 medical institutions, according to Reuters.

item.title: Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story
item.description:
Source: BBC News
Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing. His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated. "For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter," he posted on X, external. The accusation has caused an uproar on social media and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing. "I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner," Wakatama told the BBC's Front Row programme. The chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara's article - Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI, external - had been published on Sunday. It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies. Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was "well founded and reasonable" but she said Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong. The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers. Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time "to fight this literary stop-and-frisk", external. Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how "these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers" and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised. "Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?" she added. Wakatama said as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize Kundizeza would be sending in documentation about his various drafts and there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025, external. In his statement, Kundizeza said had "a concrete, documented history" about the story's inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development. Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, which are all previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched that their work was original. She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but what she was against was "it being used as a final arbiter in this case". I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready" Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was "not yet tested". "I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready." Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, "including one as good of Pangram" was "not going to be 100% accurate". In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels, external, which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to English-language writing by non-native English speakers. The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered "as an initial flag for further investigation". Vara told BBC's Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment "to suss out these things" and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human". "I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it's so different from this story, as if the same person hadn't written both." In response Kundizeza wrote: "To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing." For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using "X but Y", which she says is common in AI-generated texts. "Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come," is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother. "The proliferation of those struck me," Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had a lot of metaphors, also prevalent in writing generated by AI. The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks. He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began. "Much like the father in the story, my own dad... was an accountant, but he quit his job to grow tomatoes. So it kind of touches on both of our fathers," he told BBC Newsday. On X, Kundizeza said he was heartened by "the numerous messages of solidarity from fellow writers and readers", ending his message by saying: "Most importantly, I will continue to write." You may also be interested in: Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.

item.title: Horrified witnesses recount fatal rollercoaster incident at Six Flags
item.description:
Source: BBC News
Warning: This article contains some graphic details One person has died and others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia. The Cobb County Police Department is investigating Monday's death at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta. The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers. Horrified witnesses have told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride and police say preliminary information indicates this was the case. Six Flags said it was temporarily closing nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution. It said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones". The Cobb County Police Department said the incident happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday. It said officers working at the park found the man, identified as Atlanta resident Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, beneath the ride. He was unresponsive and not breathing. "Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction," police said in a statement. The Office of Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire, which enforces amusement park safety rules and standards in Georgia, said it was also reviewing the incident "to ensure full compliance with all applicable policies and procedures". Local CNN affiliate WXIA quoted a witness saying Kariem had come loose from his seat and had then struck the rollercoaster and some of his fellow riders before falling onto the roof of a nearby haunted house attraction. The incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion, the witness added. A husband and wife, who were on the ride, also told WXIA that Kariem fell from the ride and was struck by it. They said workers at the park had checked their safety harnesses before the ride set off. "We were having a great time and to just screaming 'Oh my God, what is happening?'," the woman said. Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she was in line to ride Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a girl covered in blood. Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off". Brittany Landry, who believes she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears. "I broke because we were just on there," she said. A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately and that they were cooperating on an investigation into the incident. Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was also coordinating with local police and park security on the situation. The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims. The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five. Brian Avery, a University of Florida professor with an expertise in amusement ride and device operations, told the BBC that rollercoasters are not federally regulated, leaving it up to states to determine the necessary safety protocols and maintenance procedures. "When these types of tragedies happen, you got to get to the bottom as to why, so we can move forward and address those issues so that they never happen again," Avery said. He explained that one of the main factors considered when designing a rollercoaster is how to contain the rider. This specifically includes determining where to place their harness - something that changes depending on the ride type. "We design these rides, the industry does, to flirt with danger," Avery said. "We're taking people up to the edge, but we're not actually putting them in danger. That is the goal." Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico. The death in Georgia comes just weeks after one of Six Flags' parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride. Six Flags said that ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire the attraction because it was "the right thing to do". - Were you at Six Flags? item.title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
item.description:
Source: BBC News
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV." Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia. "I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer." Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner. Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact". There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country. But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives. Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that. "We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs. "For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine." "The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added. Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver. The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible. His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows. There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles. Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile. "After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC. She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult. But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood. "I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him. Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits. Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic. "Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards." She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves. "So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious." At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection. Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee. "If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect." Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province. "We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said. The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month. He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said. "We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her." After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude. "The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback." Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity. Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly. "It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said. "I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy. "I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

item.title: Who's to blame for the toxic smog choking South East Asia?
item.description:
Source: BBC News
As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region. The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra has turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels. The smog - or haze - has drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia. Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland, as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them. The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El Niño: a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world. According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land. Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn". This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops. But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land. While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky. But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism". Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed. But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy over the haze. A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning. This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace. First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implements robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations". Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded. Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished. "We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said. 'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen' It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies. In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze. The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law. But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies. Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-vice-president Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset". Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads the Indonesian government's communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests". "When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans. But in the past Indonesia has also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze. This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires, though Jakarta has not officially requested international support. In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society groups to force the government to take action. In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze. They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the covering healthcare costs. A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra but was dismissed. Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have been at dangerous levels for weeks. There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day. "I'm short of breath and have a headache from breathing this air. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week. "The government must also think about common people like us. Please take action to find a solution so that this haze problem can be resolved immediately."

item.title: What we know about the man who died falling from a Six Flags rollercoaster
item.description:
Source: BBC News
Warning: This story includes distressing content A man has died after falling from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park on Monday in the US state of Georgia. The man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was found dead under the ride after being ejected and hitting other people on it, according to police. An investigation is under way and few details have yet to be released about what happened. Six Flags, the largest amusement park operator in North America, has temporarily closed nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution. Here's what we know so far about the incident. What happened? The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday. "Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday. "Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction." The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident. The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review. John King, the current commissioner who is running for re-election, said during a debate on Tuesday that "our very professional inspectors have inspected every one of those before the park season even started". "They're currently on the ground looking at every nook and cranny, conducting interviews and conducting a thorough review of what happened," he said. Officials have not held a news conference on the incident. The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five. The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones". Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground. "It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that." He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him. One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement. Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed". "Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen." He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched. Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood. Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off". Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears. "I broke because we were just on there," she said. Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer. His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death. He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach. "Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account. "His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did." Niama Kariem, who referred to him as her cousin on Facebook, wrote a lengthy tribute, saying: "Hassan, you meant so much to so many people. "You stood by both sides of your family with love and loyalty. And just as you always showed up for us, we will continue to show up for the people you loved," she wrote. "Your life was so much bigger than the tragedy that took you from us." Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website. Has this happened before? The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims. According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool. Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico. In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet. In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.

item.title: Is Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?
item.description:
Source: BBC News
Claims that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres reduced Kremlin-linked bot networks have spread widely online, but experts have told BBC Verify there is no evidence the attacks have significantly reduced them. Viral social media posts have claimed there has been a significant drop in influence operations in recent days, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky suggesting on Monday there was "less hate, less division and fewer provocations" online because of "fewer bots". Russian influence operations, which promote pro-Kremlin narratives and spread disinformation, have been tracked by researchers and journalists including BBC Verify for more than a decade. These campaigns push disinformation on to people's social media feeds on issues like the Ukraine war or post messages in support of Moscow's interests. Ukraine has struck three of Russian tech giant Yandex's five data centres since 8 October in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian internet hubs. The second of these strikes on Thursday caused Yandex, often referred to as Russia's Google, to announce it was struggling to maintain its services. But claims these attacks have affected Russian disinformation operations, including accounts posting supportive messages about groups including the Make American Great Again (MAGA) movement in the US and the far-right AfD party in Germany, appear to have come from a misinterpretation of data produced by tech firm Cloudflare. Some social media users have been sharing charts of Cloudflare data which show bot activity using Yandex's network has declined. While bots are commonly associated with fake social media accounts that may post false, divisive and inflammatory content, they are also used to automate tasks like scanning web pages so they appear on search engines. Cloudflare clarified its data includes all automated internet requests to websites hosted on its network, including bots crawling websites for information. The company also said the drop off was "not necessarily bot behaviour on social media platforms". Tomáš Zdechovský, a Czech member of the European Parliament, shared a post on X which has been viewed more than four million times, that said: "If confirmed, this is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets." He has since said he "did not present it as a clear fact", but the post remains pinned at the top of his X profile. Researchers from dTeam, a US-based group that tracks Moscow-linked influence operations, told BBC Verify there has not been "any traffic change from known Russian accounts and bot clusters on any platform". They added that if the offices of known groups involved in these operations "were in flames then we would see a change". Bots linked to pro-Kremlin influence operations like Storm-1516 and Matryoshka - both of which BBC Verify has previously reported on - were still active on social media on Tuesday, evidence shared with BBC Verify by dTeam shows. Zelensky's office told BBC Verify the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity. It added it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users. Mikhail Klimarev, an independent internet analyst, told BBC Russian that while Cloudflare can establish whether bots or real people have visited a website it does not reflect what these bots are doing. He added that Yandex uses bots to "essentially crawl the entire internet once a day" and index websites for search engine purposes, so it is most likely the company switched these off in response to its computing resources being severely degraded. Yandex has said the use of its cloud services for "large-scale manipulation on social media, spam and other improper activities" are against its rules and that accounts which violate this are blocked. While there is no evidence to conclude the strikes on Yandex's data centres have had an impact on Russia's influence operations, they have disrupted internet services for many. Isik Mater, director of research at the internet monitoring group Netblocks, told BBC Verify disruptions related to Ukrainian strikes "affect all users" globally and "websites which rely on Yandex may be partially or entirely unusable". She said that following Ukraine's attacks there has been a clear impact on the company's cloud services and platforms relying on them, adding that an entire area remaining "out of service indicates a significant infrastructure-level incident rather than a brief service interruption".

item.title: First Santa Ana winds of the season bring fire danger to L.A. Thursday and Friday
item.description:
Source: LA Times
First Santa Ana winds of the season bring fire danger to L.A. Thursday and Friday - Southern California’s first Santa Ana winds of the season will intensify Thursday and Friday, with gusts reaching 60 mph — and up to 70 mph in mountain areas. - Red-flag warnings cover much of Los Angeles and Ventura counties, where dry vegetation, low humidity and heat could help new fires spread quickly, especially west of the 405 Freeway. - Malibu residents may face power shutoffs, while coastal temperatures in the 90s bring a risk of heat illness through Saturday. The season’s first Santa Ana wind event will begin Wednesday and ramp up Thursday, bringing significant fire risk to parched Los Angeles County. Between Thursday afternoon and Friday afternoon, large swaths of Southern California will see sustained winds of 20 to 40 mph and gusts from 40 to 60 mph, according to Ryan Kittell, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Oxnard. In the windiest mountain locations, gusts could reach 70 mph, he said. “In this environment where it’s going to be windy but also dry and warm” — with humidity between 5% and 15% in much of the region and high temperatures of 85 to 95 degrees — fire risk will be a major concern, he said. “Adding to that, the plants are very dry.” Although Southern California got some rain Sunday and Monday, most of it fell in areas south of Los Angeles County, Kittell said, leaving Los Angeles and Ventura counties very dry. “There’s a high risk for any new fires to grow really fast,” he said. The weather service issued red-flag warnings for most of Los Angeles and Ventura counties that will be in effect Thursday and Friday. Areas west of the 405 Freeway are at a greater risk for wildfire than those east of the 405, which benefited from rain from post-Tropical Storm Rachel, said Daniel Swain, UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist. Some places received 2 to 5 inches of rain, while others in Southern California got essentially no rain. “West of that point, almost no rain fell at all, and in early October we had a record-breaking heat wave,” Swain said. “East of the 405 in Southern California, the fire risk is lower because it recently rained.” The fire risk isn’t nearly as bad as in January 2025, just prior to the devastating Eaton and Palisades fires, which destroyed much of Altadena and Pacific Palisades, Swain said. Still, there are concerns. “This is not January 2025. The winds are not going to be anywhere near as strong. They will not be as widespread. The vegetation is not as dry. So every single factor is less extreme than in January 2025,” Swain said. “The risk is not going to be as high, and it will be more localized because some places have seen recent rain.” But in places that have remained dry, there will be risks. In those “pockets,” Swain said, “this will be potentially a fairly high-end event. So on the western side of the L.A. metro [area], into Ventura, Santa Barbara counties, the risk is still potentially pretty high. ... It just hasn’t really rained there much yet this season, and there was recent record heat, and the wind will be pretty strong. So there may be public safety power shutoffs.” Southern California Edison warned Malibu residents that it might shut down power on four major circuits beginning Thursday at midnight, the city of Malibu said in a written statement. The city of Calabasas said in a statement Tuesday that Southern California Edison might cut power because of strong winds and wildfire risk. The shutoff could take place as soon as Wednesday, according to the city. On Tuesday evening, Southern California Edison’s online dashboard said it was considering public safety shutoffs for more than 220,000 customers — roughly 4.5% of its total customers — because of heightened wildfire risk. The company is considering shutoffs in Kern, Los Angeles, Santa Barbara, Tulare and Ventura counties. San Diego Gas and Electric has not announced public safety shutoffs, according to the company’s dashboard. The weather service issued some wind advisories and high-wind warnings in the mountains to highlight that “the wind itself could cause issues like downed power lines, power outages, road hazards and general nuisance,” Kittell said. In addition to the wind, the hottest conditions will be along the coast, where temperatures will be in the 90s. “There’s a high risk for heat illness Thursday through Saturday,” Kittell said, as many residents do not have air conditioning in coastal areas.

item.title: Burbank airport's new $1.3-billion terminal opens — bigger and sleeker than ever
item.description:
Source: LA Times
After 33 months of construction and $1.3 billion in spending, the Hollywood Burbank Airport’s new terminal opened on Tuesday morning, with a medley of arrivals and departures in the minutes after 7 a.m. Instead of the snug, historic facility whose Spanish Colonial Revival style dated to 1930, travelers found themselves in a sleek terminal at Winona Avenue and Hollywood Way, distinguished by high ceilings, contemporary art, twinkling terrazzo floors, abundant charging stations and landscaping full of cactus and succulents, along with a few “wet paint” signs. Passengers gawked at mirrored grid artwork by Glenn Kaino overhead. “It was weird,” said Tanya Radke, 25, of Van Nuys, who was headed to Kansas City, Mo., and caught off guard by the terminal switch. “It was not what I thought was going to happen today for me.” But looking around, the passenger called the new space a big upgrade. “It reminds me a lot of the Kansas City airport,” Radke said. “It was well overdue.” The day’s schedule called for about 90 departures and arrivals by eight airlines, roughly the same schedule as in the previous buildings. The new terminal also has the same two runways and same number of gates — 14 — as the airport’s previous two-terminal alignment. And passengers still often board planes from the front and back, using outdoor steps from the tarmac, rather than enclosed tunnels. That practice is something travelers have long praised for its informality and efficiency. But the new building does bring many changes. It measures about 50% larger than the two old terminals combined — about 355,000 square feet — with higher ceilings and a pair of illuminated steel sculptures by Cliff Garten flanking the main entrance. The first departure was Alaska Flight 3401 to Santa Rosa, Calif., at 7:03 a.m. with 33 passengers aboard. The first arrival: Southwest Flight 189 from Las Vegas, which landed at 7:16 a.m. with 30 passengers aboard. “The taxi off was a little different. Instead of turning right, you turn left,” said Southwest Airlines pilot Mike Petros, who arrived at 7:31 a.m. with a planeload of passengers from Sacramento. At the start of the flight, Petros said, “We told them that we would be flying to a new terminal, so if they had anybody picking them up, let them know.” Still, many were surprised. Airport management deployed several staffers to redirect confused travelers from the old terminals (now idle) to the new one. Anthony Bailey, 29, said he learned of the switch from an Uber driver on his way to the airport. “So far, I’m liking it,” Bailey said of the new terminal, standing near Gate 13 before catching a flight to Las Vegas. “Nice and clean. The TSA line was pretty smooth.” While most of the six retail stores were open Tuesday, none of the terminal’s 13 food concessions were fully operating. Two eateries were offering grab-and-go options, and airport spokesperson Mike Christensen said more options would arrive later in the day and week. When the new terminal concessions open, dining options will include Guy Fieri’s Flavor Town, Spring Chicken, Diane’s Farm Table and Italian Market, Jones Coffee, Perry’s Joint, Poquito Mas, West Coast Smash Burgers, Massis Kabob, Starbucks, Border Grill, Jet Tila’s Asian Table, Santa Canela bakery and a bar, Pete’s Pub, with picture-window views of the runways and Verdugo Mountains. Many travelers, including William Langlois and Annie Cerillo of Tampa, Fla., noted the shortage of eating options Tuesday. “It’s horrible, there’s no restaurants and not enough security stations,” said Langlois, who had gone to the old terminal first and was redirected. Before this change, “this was the easiest airport,” Cerillo said. In the new terminal, airport officials say, the walk from the entrance to the farthest gate is 1,285 feet, down from 1,600 feet, with wider corridors and sidewalks and access to power plugs for devices from every seat. (Its many charging stations are now mostly USB-C ports, not USB.) The new terminal includes eight Transportation Security Administration lines, versus five in the old setup. Baggage claim carousels have moved from outdoors to indoors. The airport’s new parking structure includes about 2,000 spots and 310 charging ports for electric vehicles. (The airport’s total number of parking spaces is 6,637, the same as before.) As it did before, the airport supplies shuttle bus service between the new terminal and Burbank Airport-South Train Station (which connects with Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner) and the Burbank Airport-North Station at San Fernando Road and Hollywood Way. Among many preparations for the day, airport officials staged a “passenger simulation trial” on Sept. 19, inviting 1,500 volunteers to behave like passengers in the new building, giving dozens of airport workers, including TSA staffers and airline gate agents, a chance to prepare for Tuesday. The airport, second busiest in L.A. County, was built in 1930 and is run by the Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority. For decades it has been favored by many local travelers as a simpler, faster, quainter alternative to Los Angeles International Airport. The Burbank airport’s site in the San Fernando Valley, however, has often put its leaders at odds with residents of surrounding suburban neighborhoods. Unlike LAX, which has no flight curfew, the Burbank airport has limited operating hours — 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Before this week’s move, the aged Burbank facility didn’t meet current state seismic standards or Federal Aviation Administration design standards, which prompted repeated safety warnings. Airport officials said the new design also increases the distance between the terminal and the nearest runway, formerly as little as 257 feet, to about 880 feet — a change that brings the airport into compliance with FAA standards. Voters approved the Burbank airport terminal replacement project in 2016. Construction began in 2024. The airport reported about 6.2 million arriving and departing passengers in 2025, flying to and from about 30 nonstop destinations. “It’s a beautiful building, but buildings aren’t anything without people who fill them with dedication and service,” said Tyron Hampton, president of the airport authority and City Council member in Pasadena. He predicted that the new facility would attract not only new passengers but also new businesses to the commercial corridor along Burbank’s Winona Avenue. As Burbank unveils its new terminal, the opening of LAX’s most high-profile project — the SkyLink automated people mover (a 2.25-mile electric train route linking terminals to rail service and rental cars) has been delayed by technical and legal issues until Jan. 6 at the earliest. “I don’t like to compare,” said Hampton when asked about LAX. “We have 14 gates. LAX has 161.”

item.title: Suspicious bags at Disneyland prompt bomb squad response, evacuation
item.description:
Source: LA Times
Suspicious bags at Disneyland prompt bomb squad response, evacuation Two suspicious bags left near the main entrance to Disneyland prompted a bomb squad response Monday night, officials said. Disneyland security alerted the Anaheim Police Department at about 9:50 p.m. to two bags someone had left near a roundabout, including one with marbles inside and wires sticking out of it and another with duct tape on top and sharp instruments sticking out of it, Sgt. Eric Anderson said. One of the bags was on a dolly. Officers evacuated Disneyland visitors, directing them to another exit, and requested assistance from the Orange County Sheriff’s Department bomb squad to check out the bags. Shortly before midnight, the squad determined the bags were harmless and contained no explosives, Anderson said. Police believe the bags were left intentionally to look suspicious, Anderson said, and are looking for whomever was responsible.

item.title: Six Flags Magic Mountain shuts down second coaster amid safety concerns, rider death in Georgia
item.description:
Source: LA Times
Six Flags Magic Mountain shuts down second coaster amid safety concerns, rider death in Georgia Six Flags is closing several attractions across the U.S. and Canada — including the Goliath roller coaster at Magic Mountain in Valencia — after a man fell to his death from a ride at one of its parks in Georgia. Officials said the temporary closures were “out of an abundance of caution.” On Monday afternoon, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, of Atlanta, was ejected from a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia and struck other riders as he fell, the Cobb County Police Department said in a statement. Kariem landed beneath the roller coaster, where police officers found him just before 4 p.m., unconscious and not breathing. The Police Department’s major crimes unit is investigating. Park officials closed the Goliath roller coaster at the Georgia park and similar attractions at its other locations after the fatal incident. Six Flags did not confirm whether Kariem fell from the Goliath, but Georgia television news stations aired video of passengers being evacuated from the ride Monday afternoon.
