One rider told Atlanta NBC affiliate 11Alive that Kariem’s fall was captured in rider souvenir photographs that are automatically taken as their train passes. “He was in our pictures,” the unnamed person told the news station. “He fell and hit the car three different times.” Kariem was an information technology manager at Wesley International Academy, a public K-8 charter school, and “a cherished” member of the staff “whose presence and impact will be deeply missed by our students, staff, and all those whose lives he touched,” Atlanta Public Schools said in a statement Tuesday. Six Flags announced this week that, in addition to Goliath in Georgia, it had closed the following rides: - Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia - Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Gurnee, Ill. - Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in Jackson Township, N.J. - Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada’s Wonderland in Vaughan, Ontario - Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds in Charlotte, N.C. - Orion and Diamondback at Kings Island in Kings Island, Ohio The company did not elaborate on why these specific rides were chosen, but noted they were “similar.” Magic Mountain’s Goliath roller coaster opened in 2000 and is described on the park’s website as a “metal monster” — reaching speeds of up to 85 mph while taking riders down a 255-foot plunge at a 61-degree angle, “one of the longest and fastest drops in the world.” The Georgia version, which this year marked its 20th anniversary, tops out at 70 mph and reaches 200 feet in height, according to its online ride profile. The closures come less than a month after Magic Mountain announced the permanent closure of its acclaimed X2 ride, the first roller coaster in the world that spun riders 360 degrees in their seats. The attraction was retired in late September after multiple people sued the theme park operator, alleging they suffered brain injuries on the ride and that Six Flags had failed to adequately warn them of the risk. X2 had been closed since July, following reports of back-to-back brain injuries. In June 2022, Christopher Hawley had trouble walking immediately after riding the roller coaster, then lost consciousness. Doctors found severe brain bleeding. He died the next day, and a coroner’s report cited head trauma from a “park ride accident,” according to a 2023 lawsuit filed against Magic Mountain by his family, who settled for an undisclosed amount this summer. “While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Brian Oerding, Six Flags Magic Mountain president, said in a statement last month, adding that “ride safety is a cornerstone of our business.” Georgia’s Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire, the state agency that regulates and inspects theme parks, said in a statement Tuesday that it is “actively investigating” the fatal incident. Six Flags Over Georgia, located in the Atlanta suburb of Austell, is “a significant part” of the region’s tourism industry, “drawing visitors from across our county, our state, and the Southeast,” Lisa Cupid, chairwoman of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners, said in a statement. “We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories,” she wrote. Martin Lewison, an associate professor at Farmingdale State College in New York who researches theme parks and has ridden more than 2,600 roller coasters around the world, said he has boarded the Goliath in Georgia many times. Its manufacturer, the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, “is highly respected ... and has a stellar safety record,” he said. “These Bolliger & Mabillard hypercoasters are super popular, they’re all over the world, and they’re fun,” he said. “It’s a real tragedy to have this workhorse of the roller coaster thrill world be involved.” The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The manufacturer of the Goliath in Valencia was Giovanola — a now-defunct Swiss company. Lewison, who noted he is a Six Flags shareholder, said that when the company’s theme parks close for several weeks in the winter, each ride is thoroughly inspected, with the safety restraints carefully evaluated and “every bolt and every metal plate” checked for fatigue. “A lot of people in the theme park industry and the enthusiast community are scratching their heads because ... a restraint failure is so unusual and unlikely,” he said of the Georgia tragedy. Dennis Speigel, owner and founder of the Cincinnati-based consulting firm International Theme Park Services, said more more than 380 million people visit theme and amusement parks in North America annually, adding up to nearly 2 billion rides. In 2024, there were an estimated 118 serious injuries requiring hospital visits, he said. Speigel said theme parks are statistically very safe “due to the self-policing, the state inspections, the insurance inspections and the third-party inspections that are done.” He called Six Flags’ decision to shut down the rides in question “absolutely the proper approach” to ensure safety. “This will not deter people from coming to the park,” he said. “It never has. They will come back as soon as that ride is put back into operation, and the lines will be longer than they have before. I’ve seen that over and over, for decades.” In 2024, Six Flags Entertainment Corp. merged with Cedar Fair, the company that owns Knott’s Berry Farm in Buena Park. The combined company sold seven parks this year as it worked to pay down about $5 billion in debt.

item.title: L.A. community horrified after beloved dog found hanging from leash. 'No words can describe it'
item.description:
Source: LA Times
L.A. community horrified after beloved dog found hanging from leash. ‘No words can describe it’ On a recent Sunday, resident Filiberto Reyes thought his beloved husky had once again gotten out of the fenced front yard. Hours later, a neighbor showed him a disturbing video circulating online of a dog that had been hanged in a Lynwood alley less than a mile from Reyes’ home. It was Ruso, he said. “It’s like losing a son,” Reyes told The Times on Monday night. “The way he died. ... No words can describe it.” He exhaled. The 9-year-old husky was described by Reyes as a playful dog who was gentle with children. Ruso liked to stand up on his hind paws to hug people using his front paws, Reyes said. Reyes didn’t see the incident that neighbors said unfolded the afternoon of Oct. 4. A man and a woman were seen outside the fence, he said. The woman was bitten by the dog, and the pair let the dog out of the yard, luring him out with food, according to Reyes. Reyes believes the pair agitated the dog, who reacted in self-defense. Ruso was found dead later that evening, hanged with an orange leash from a metal security door, according to a video shared on social media. Reyes said the dog was found behind a doughnut shop and laundromat on Long Beach Boulevard. He never saw Ruso’s body. By the time Reyes arrived at the scene on Sunday evening, authorities had taken Ruso away. Reyes said he’d seen the man he suspected was responsible in Lynwood since the incident and notified authorities. There have been no arrests. Lynwood City Councilman Luis Cuellar said he was made aware on social media of the disturbing incident and notified the city manager, who then launched an investigation. “The City of Lynwood is deeply saddened and disturbed by the reported animal cruelty incident that has caused significant concern throughout our community,” the city said in a statement released Friday. “We extend our heartfelt sympathy to the dog’s owner and to everyone affected by this deeply troubling situation.” As outcry over the incident grew online, the city issued a follow-up statement just hours later, saying it “understands the concern and sadness this reported incident has caused throughout our community.” A deputy with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department Century Station said Monday night that the department had received hundreds of emails regarding the husky’s death. The city encouraged anyone who “witnessed the incident or has video, photographs or other relevant information” to contact Det. Christina Smith at (213) 678-5402. Reyes, 34, an aerospace quality inspector, said he and his family no longer feel safe living in Compton after what happened. They are considering moving elsewhere, perhaps to Bellflower or Lakewood. He said he just wants the investigation to conclude and to get justice for Ruso.

item.title: Record-breaking hurricane activity in Pacific Ocean is battering the California coast
item.description:
Source: LA Times
Record-breaking hurricane activity in Pacific Ocean is battering the California coast - Pacific storms have generated more accumulated cyclone energy this season than ever recorded, battering Southern California beaches, homes and roads and reshaping the coastline. - El Niño and warming ocean waters are helping fuel the activity, while an exceptionally strong El Niño could bring more coastal erosion, flooding and damage this winter — especially during high tides. A season of tropical storms and hurricanes with record-breaking energy in the Pacific Ocean is battering the Southern California coastline. Researchers at Colorado State University confirmed Monday that storms this summer have generated a higher level of accumulated cyclone energy than ever recorded, surpassing the prior seasonal record set in 2018. The metric is a measure of the total wind energy, intensity and duration of tropical storms and hurricanes. “It’s been a wild season,” said Daniel Cayan, a climate researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego, noting that parts of Southern California‘s coast already have experienced significant damage ahead of any winter storms in store for the region amid the strongest El Niño on record. The historic Long Beach boardwalk buckled after a barrage of storms over the last month. As Tropical Storm Rachel approached the coast over the weekend, powerful waves slammed into oceanfront homes, leaving some on the verge of collapse. In Newport Beach, water from a massive swell — double the size that was initially predicted — blasted through 20-foot berms erected at the beach and inundated roads with about a foot of sea water ahead of Rachel’s arrival. Elsewhere along the coast, the continuous battering from higher-than-normal ocean levels and strong waves this summer has washed away sand, profoundly altering the Wedge in Newport Beach, as well as beaches in San Onofre, Laguna Beach and San Clemente. The coastal damage has been so significant that Orange County declared an emergency last month. The exceptionally active hurricane season in the Pacific is influenced by several factors including a long-term ocean heating trend caused by global warming, and higher nearshore ocean temperatures and a decrease in wind shear from El Niño, which can significantly weaken hurricane activity, UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain explained during a recent webinar. “El Niño in the Pacific Basin decreases wind shear, so it removes the inhibitive storm-decapitating effect of wind shear at the same time that it amplifies water temperature,” Swain said. “So it adds more fuel and it makes that fuel more likely to take advantage of its environment.” Typically, once storms enter the cooler water in the eastern tropical Pacific, they weaken significantly. But the marine heat wave and El Niño conditions — bringing ocean temperatures 10 to 13 degrees higher than normal — have provided a more conducive environment for hurricanes such as Rachel to get close enough to affect the California coast. These storms, combined with high tides and the Kelvin wave, which can add 6 to 12 inches to background sea levels, have resulted in significant damage and a reshaping of the coast over the summer. And it’s not over yet, experts say. Hurricane Simon, currently spinning along Mexico’s west coast, is expected to make landfall there this week, and forecasters say there’s roughly a 90% chance of another cyclone formation in the next seven days. “I wouldn’t be surprised if we saw a couple more hurricanes or tropical systems forming in the Central Pacific, South Pacific area,” said Kristan Lund, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Oxnard. Southern California also is bracing to see what El Niño has in store this winter. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center said last week that there was virtually a 100% chance that the El Niño this season will be categorized as “very strong.” There’s also an 83% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest on record, going back to 1950, up from a 75% probability forecast last month. Even if it doesn’t result in torrential rain, El Niño can wreak havoc on the coastline. Beaches typically go through a seasonal cycle with powerful winter waves dragging sand out to sea and more mild summer waves depositing the sand back onshore. But El Niño winters generally bring even stronger waves, resulting in more sand loss and erosion. “There’s likely to be pretty profound influences along the coast,” Cayan said of the months ahead. “There [are] also cliff failures and other impacts when you get these big waves that are higher and more active than normal, so there’s a lot of concern about that.” Two of the strongest El Niños in the last 75 years, in 1982-83 and 1997-98, were associated with extensive damage to the Southern California coast, battering homes, flooding streets and damaging piers. Another one — in 2015-16 — did not result in above-average rain but did cause record coastal erosion. During that winter, researchers determined that the more extreme waves were about 50% larger than usual and the level of beach erosion was 76% higher than normal. “Since that really big winter in 1983, we’ve had several occasions of pretty active winter storms, but we’ve sort of dodged bullets because those storms, in general, didn’t fall upon the highest tides,” Cayan said. “So this winter, again, it’s going to be sort of a luck of the draw.” This winter, if El Niño-fueled storms arrive during king tides, it’s likely that California will see significant coastal erosion, flooding and damage, Cayan said. King tides, which can push water levels past 7 feet, or higher during El Niño, are expected around Thanksgiving, Christmas and late January. “Those periods are really critical for the fate of the California coastline and infrastructure this winter,” Cayan said.

item.title: Here are the threats that remain from storm Rachel and the weather whiplash that comes next
item.description:
Source: LA Times
Here are the threats that remain from storm Rachel and the weather whiplash that comes next After the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel damaged coastal homes in Long Beach and brought flooding and debris flows to the Coachella Valley, National Weather Service forecasters project the worst has passed for Southern California — but threats remain for communities along the coast. Wind advisories across inland deserts were set to expire early Monday morning. Coastal flooding advisories from San Diego through San Luis Obispo, however, remain in place, with two more sets of potentially damaging high tides projected for Monday and Tuesday mornings. Currently, the most extreme high tides are occurring between 10 and 11 a.m., with milder secondary high tides between 11 p.m. and midnight. Although the morning high tides over the weekend qualified as minor flooding, the nighttime high tides did not. Preliminary readings near Long Beach measured Sunday morning’s tide around 7.6 feet. Forecasters with the weather service predicted Monday and Tuesday mornings’ tides would reach around 7.5 feet. The coastal flooding advisories farther north, in Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties, extend through Monday morning’s high tide. The advisories farther south, from San Diego to Ventura, extend through Tuesday’s. The weather service warned that additional isolated damage was possible but unlikely. Beach erosion and flooding of beach parking lots and pathways are likely. Threats also remain from strong rip currents and large waves, which increase the risk of ocean drowning and could threaten to capsize small boats near shore. On Sunday morning, a man died at Dockweiler Beach, and authorities were investigating whether he drowned due to storm conditions. The overall mellowing of the forecast comes as the extent of coastal damage remains less than what some officials feared. The impacts were severe for some homes on the Long Beach Peninsula, as the storm swept away a portion of the historic boardwalk and damaged multiple houses. But in Newport Beach, officials said the city had so far avoided major damage and flooding after working around the clock to shore up berms. Experts attribute the extremely warm ocean temperatures that fueled Rachel, which peaked as a Category 3 hurricane, in part to El Niño. UC Agriculture and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain also placed blame on a months-long marine heat wave preceding El Niño, as well as human-caused climate change. Although Rachel was only the second time in history that Southern California received a tropical storm watch, Swain said in a recent webinar it’s possible the region could see another tropical storm before hurricane season comes to an end. “It’s getting a little late, but the ocean is so warm that we can’t rule out more tropical impacts into late October, maybe even early November,” he said. Tropical Storm Rachel, for example, brought more than 6 inches of rain to parts of San Diego County and more than 2 inches of rain to some L.A. County mountains over the weekend, according to preliminary data released Monday by the National Weather Service. But looking forward, the National Weather Service forecasts Southern California will swing to the other side of the spectrum by the end of the week: high temperatures, dry air and some of the first Santa Ana winds of the season are expected, carrying a heightened potential for wildfires. The fire weather is projected to begin Thursday and last through Saturday.

item.title: What it will take for the Griffith Park merry-go-round to finally spin again
item.description:
Source: LA Times
- The city of Los Angeles last year purchased the Griffith Park merry-go-round for $1 million. It has been closed for years. - Plans are being drawn to have the carousel operational again in a matter of years, this time with a little help from those in the theme park industry. Nestled a short stroll from the Griffith Park Ranger Station, near some tennis courts and not far from the remains of the park’s original zoo, lies a gem that is on most days behind lock and key. The Griffith Park merry-go-round, which turned 100 this year, stands motionless, many of its 66 wooden horses weathered and caught mid-ascent. But the effort to ensure that they once again rise, fall and spin around a spherical base has begun. The Griffith Park merry-go-round is being resurrected by a group of passionate supporters and volunteers, some of whom are veterans of the theme park industry. Collectively, they argue that this isn’t simply a relic from another era but a place of multigenerational connection, a reminder of the beauty of handmade art and a statement piece of Los Angeles. Closed since the COVID-19 pandemic, save for a brief but limited run in 2022, the Griffith Park carousel is now under city control, purchased last year for $1 million. That’s a veritable bargain for such a museum piece, argues Tracy James, who is leading the efforts to restore the project, one that’s expected to take at least two years and cost millions. “This is the jewel in the middle of the city,” says James, who works in the Department of Recreation and Parks and focuses on Griffith Park. “The ornamentation and the craftsmanship represent a bygone era.” There was a real fear, James says, that the merry-go-round would fall into the hands of a private collector, as the carousel, if not officially, has long symbolically belonged to L.A. A piece of whimsy, artistry and play in the middle of a natural wonderland, it is where Walt Disney is said to have dreamed up the vision for what would become Disneyland and a site that has witnessed civil rights actions and 1960s-era love-ins. To some, it’s a beacon of hope in the midst of an imperfect urban fabric that has long prioritized the fantastical. “I got teary-eyed when I walked up,” says Wendy Osmundson, who approached the carousel while on a stroll around the park during a recent open house. Osmundson reflected on a day, decades ago, when the merry-go-round saved the family’s Christmas. 1. Details from the Griffith Park merry-go-round, which is in need of refurbishment. 2. The horses of the Griffith Park merry-go-round are known for their flowing manes. 3. Each horse at the carousel is outfitted with jewels. “I was 21, and my mom’s kitchen burned down,” Osmundson says. “We couldn’t have Christmas at my mom’s house. Everyone came to my one-bedroom apartment in Los Feliz, and me and my three sisters came here and rode the carousel. We were adults, but it was really great. I’d love to see it restored.” Joining the project to do just that are some of the brightest minds in the theme park and amusement industry, and they’re doing so without pay and on their own time. Kurt Sawitskas has already spent weeks analyzing the carousel’s innards, marveling at its antique nature, but also amazed that it’s still mostly intact. “Honestly, I don’t think carousels were ever intended to last 100 years,” Sawitskas says. “And now here we are with a carousel that’s 100 years old. We want to honor it and make it run again.” Sawitskas’ day job is at Walt Disney Imagineering, the creative arm of the company responsible for theme park design. Beginning to think ahead toward retirement, Sawitskas says he was looking for a project in which he could volunteer his time and expertise. He found it. Built in 1926, near the end of what many consider the heyday of the American carousel, the Griffith Park merry-go-round began its life in San Diego and was relocated to Los Angeles in the depths of the Great Depression in 1937. It is the showcase product of the Spillman Engineering Co., whose carousel horses were known for the flowing, wind-blown manes and heavily detailed secondary carvings on the portion of their bodies that face viewers, known as the “romance” side. A few, for instance, have lion heads extending from their chest. Others have cherubs reaching toward the horse’s face. All are adorned with jewels and tails made of real horsehair, many of which have been eaten by squirrels or other critters. Griffith Park’s carousel is especially unique in that it also has horses from master carvers Charles Looff and Charles Carmel, considered the finest carousel craftsmen of the era. The few carousel companies that survived the Depression largely did so by switching to a cheaper, mass-produced product, such as transitioning from wood to aluminum. An art was lost. “It’s brought to me a real appreciation of the deeper aesthetic,” Sawitskas says. He mentions this as he’s giving a tour of the horses, emphasizing how the thickness of the paint created a sense of depth in the figures — a saddle, for instance, of a crisscrossing chessboard-like pattern, or elsewhere an aged leathery toughness. “I recognize what is attractive about an amusement like this, and that’s the ability to return again and again and still see something different.” Sawitskas has recruited a pair of co-workers, Troy Leverton and Pim Renting, who work in various aspects of ride engineering, to help in the task. For Leverton, restoring the carousel is important in bringing a piece of history back to the city, one centered on affordable outdoor entertainment. “I brought my nieces here 10-plus years ago, and rode it and it was really cool,” Leverton says. “Unfortunately, since my daughter has been born, this has been shut down. So it was like, you know what, I live in the city, and it’d be really cool to be a part of something that is doing something for the city. I want to bring my daughter back here when it is running.” It’s also not lost on them that there’s an association between the company they work for and the carousel, although it’s important to stress they are not volunteering their time as representatives of the Walt Disney Co. “There’s obviously a connection with Walt Disney and what we do,” Leverton says. “There’s a lot of history here. The industry was born out of Disneyland, and Disneyland was born out of this place.” The story goes that Disney would bring his daughters to the merry-go-round, sit on a bench and dream of a place where adults and children could be entertained together. Both Disney and the company have long told this tale, and a bench, as well as one of the original horses from the carousel, can be found on Disneyland’s Main Street, U.S.A. (There were initially 68 horses, but one, says James, is at Disneyland, and another is with a former owner.) With Disneyland’s King Arthur Carousel, which itself dates to the 1920s, Disney requested a number of modifications that closely match the Griffith Park attraction, such as wanting all its animals to be “jumpers” that look as if they’re galloping. James, along with Sawitskas and his pals, want the carousel to be restored to its original glory, a magnificent, gleaming merry-go-round that inspired Disney to dream. On a recent Saturday, Sawitskas hopped on a ladder to analyze the condition of the mechanisms that raise and lower the horses and started poring over carousel history books to match the horses with their original paint colors. In the 1920s, lead paint was used, which must be stripped away. “There’s no way to just keep painting over this and hiding the problem,” Sawitskas says. “We really need to get down to the bottom. A lot of the horses have small fractures in the wood joints that need to be repaired as well. You can’t do that on top of paint. You need to be at the wood. We have some very nice ways to get down to the wood without destroying the wood itself, just lifting the paint off. We want to restore all the worn wood and reintroduce the carving lines.” And that says nothing of the mechanical adjustments and efforts to make the carousel compliant with the Americans With Disabilities Act. The Griffith Park carousel has one speed — 14 mph — and the hope is to update it with some modern controls to create a smoother ride. All of this is why James is estimating the tally to restore the carousel will top $3 million or $4 million. An assessment is expected in the coming weeks, and fundraising will occur via the nonprofit Friends of Griffith Park. James will be hosting open houses on as many Saturdays as she can, posting updates on the Griffith merry-go-round project Instagram page. As the world turned, so did the carousel. In 1961, for instance, a riot erupted at the merry-go-round when police officers alleged a 17-year-old Black rider failed to pay for his admission. Onlookers leaped to the teen’s defense, and it took 75 officers to quell the disturbance. Later that decade, hippie love-ins were held regularly at the base of the carousel, occasionally drawing the likes of the Hells Angels or law enforcement. The merry-go-round also became a gathering spot for a candlelight vigil when the Grateful Dead’s Jerry Garcia died in 1995. And today, even in its shuttered and bruised state, it stands defiantly — a testament to handmade art at a time the world is spinning toward all-digital everything. “One of the biggest challenges here is making it look new again,” Sawitskas says. “But I think if we do that, it’s going to be a treasure.” One that, by the time it’s operational, will twirl gallantly into its next century.

item.title: Houthis launch fresh wave of missiles across Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle
These updates have been closed. Below, you can review headlines from the Saudi-Houthi conflict and elsewhere in the Middle East from Wednesday, October 14, 2026: - Fire breaks out at Aramco headquarters in Dhahran - Four injured because of debris in Saudi capital Riyadh - Fuel facility in Sanaa hit by Saudi-led coalition forces US military destroyed Iran-affiliated vessel in Gulf of Oman, CENTCOM says US forces destroyed an Iran-affiliated vessel in the Gulf of Oman last week, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Wednesday. CENTCOM said the vessel was conducting surveillance and targeting US Navy ships. The ship's crew members were safely removed from the vessel before the attack, the military command said. Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has sharply decreased since the war in Iran broke out. The strait, bordered by Iran, is key in connecting major oil producers to the rest of the world. Houthis again claim to have targeted Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport A Houthi military spokesman said on Wednesday evening that the Iran-backed group had targeted Riyadh's international airport with a ballistic missile. The comments came hours after the Saudi-led coalition reported intercepting a ballistic missile fired towards the capital, though it wasn't entirely clear if the two sides were talking about the same incident. "Our armed forces were able to taget Khalid International Airport in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, with a ballistic missile, and the strike was precise and direct," Yahya Saree wrote on X. The airport has come under repeated fire since an attack on Saturday that killed 12 people. The Houthi spokesman Saree also claimed three other ballistic missile stikes in other areas "resulting in a large number of dead and wounded, as well as the disabling of several vehicles," saying they hit "enemy mobilization points." Saudi authorities have not reported any deaths as a result of Houthi strikes on Wednesday. Saudi Arabia postpones 'Six Kings Slam' tennis tournament Saudi Arabia has postponed a high-profile exhibition tennis tournament that was scheduled to take place next week, as Houthi attacks on the country continue to create major security concerns. The "Six Kings Slam" has been postponed until December 27-30, organizers said on Wednesday in a statement that went to impressive lengths not to refer to the conflict or potential security risks in any way. "The decision reflects Riyadh Season's commitment to delivering sporting events to the highest standards, following an assessment of the organizational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and their potential impact on the quality of the audience experience," organizers said. The tournament was originally slated for October 21-24. Carlos Alacaraz, Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev, Taylor Fritz, Alex de Minaur and Learner Tien were originally scheduled to compete, after defending champion Jannik Sinner withdrew with an injury. However doubts about the likelihood of the stars traveling to the tournament amid the current security situation were already rife. The Six Kings Slam is a men-only exhibition tournament not a ranking event, but it's a high profile end-of-season competition streamed on Netflix whose large prize purse tends to attract the world's best players. Other Saudi sporting events could in theory be in doubt, including the Saudi International golf tournament in Riyadh next month, and later the 2027 Asian Cup football competition. This year's F1 Saudi Arabian Grand Prix was canceled amid the war in Iran, even before Houthi military activity against Saudi Arabia specifically intensified. Jeddah is again on the 2027 calendar, scheduled for March 19-21. Red Cross warns that Yemen's hospitals are at capacity The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has cautioned that Yemen's hospitals are finding it difficult to cope with the skyrocketing amount of war injuries as fighting intensifies across the country. Small hospitals in front-line areas in Marib and Taiz are seeing some 700 casualties of the conflict in a single week, a far great number than their usual amount of patients. "Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure," ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement. Only a handful of hospitals in Yemen are capable of handling intensive care patients, and even those lack many of the necessary supplies and medicines as other health facilities across the country. At least 200,000 people have been displaced in the conflict, further complicating matters for Yemen's still-functional hospitals. Moreover, due to changing front lines on multiple fronts, international organizations say at least 800,000 people have become cut off from much-needed humanitarian aid. Civilians in the Saudi capital Riyadh reported hearing an explosion above their city as the govenment claimed in intercepted a ballistic missile launched from Yemen. The Houthis then claimed they had again struck Riyadh airport as well as an Aramco oil refinery, something Saudi authorities have not confirmed. The increase in attacks on Saudi soil has increased pressure on Riyadh's allies, including the United States, to evaluate whether they should join the coalition against the Houthis more directly. IMF warns attacks on Saudi could impact people "everywhere" The recent attacks on Saudi Arabia could affect people adversely "everywhere," as conflict in the energy-rich region could lead to a range of economic concerns, International Monetary Fund (IMF) head Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday. The escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has sparked fears of aggravating global crises that could impact global growth, with energy markets already disrputed due to the ongoing conflict between Iran and the US. "The Saudi economy is important for the region and the world," IMF managing director Georgieva said at a news conference during the Annual Meetings of the Fund and World Bank in Bangkok. "In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere," she said. Aramco offices catches fire after suspected Houthi attack Saudi Arabia said that an attack on the headquarters of oil state oil firm Aramco sparked a "limited fire." The fire at the building at Aramco's complex in the eastern city of Dhahran resulted in no casualties or deaths, the country's Energy Ministry said. A company source told the Reuters news agency that a ballistic missile struck the top floors of an office building. The complex in Dhahran serves as a major operation for Aramco, which is the world's largest oil company. Hours earlier, Saudi authorities said they had intercepted several missiles, including over the capital city Riyadh. Several injured by fallen missile debris in Riyadh Four people were injured as a result of falling debris following two intercepted Houthi missile attacks, Saudi authorities said. According to the country's civil defense agency, two women, a man and a child were injured in the capital Riyadh, with 15 homes suffering damage. This came after residents heard a powerful explosion in the Saudi capital, with an alert being sent to their phones warning of a "hostile aerial threat." Saudi-led coalition strikes Sanaa fuel facility The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis struck targets in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa on Tuesday, Houthi-run broadcaster Al Masirah said. Locals reported hearing strong explosions in the city hours after a coalition spokesperson urged people to leave the all-Suhaba fuel facility, which belongs to the Yemeni Oil Company, and a nearby site ahead of a strike. According to a coalition spokesperson, the Houthis were using the facility for storing missiles and drones. The facility is located on a hill overlooking Sanaa. The company said the storage facilities at the site were empty, with a strike not affecting oil reserves or supplies to residents. We will be following all the latest updates from the escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen-based militant group, the Houthis. The compound of energy company Aramco saw a fire break out, the Saudi Ministry of Energy said. Saudi authorities also reported four injuries as a result of missile debris falling over Riyadh. Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen continued its strikes on Tuesday by targeting oil facilities west of capital Sanaa, the local Houthi-run broadcaster said. Join us as we bring you the latest.

item.title: Iran seeking 'harder targets' for attacks abroad, UK warns
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle
The leader of the UK's MI5 domestic security service on Tuesday said that Iran is expanding the scope of the hybrid attacks that it coordinates in the UK and elsewhere. In an annual address outlining his assessment of threats to the UK, MI5 chief Ken McCallum said a "major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites." The remarks come after the US removed about a dozen long-range bombers from Fairford air base in the southern UK last week following an incident on September 27 during which several men were arrested on "suspicion of terrorism offenses." An investigation is ongoing. Uptick in 'Iran-linked operations' McCallum said these kinds of incidents were "not unique," warning that Tehran is seeking targets beyond Iranian diaspora living abroad who oppose the regime. These include Iranian media organizations, Israeli interests in the UK, and arson attacks on Jewish sites that British authorities say were carried out by Iranian proxies. The spy chief warned of an "unflinching response" to "those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets – whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas." He added that more than 50 people have been arrested in "Iran-linked operations" in the UK over the past year. However, McCallum said Iran's ability to carry out more severe and complex attacks using explosive drones remains limited by the sophistication of the proxies and criminals it has used for operations in the UK. UK says Fairford air base incident likely coordinated by Iran On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the suspected plot at Fairford air base was coordinated in Iran and was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC). The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited. Seven suspects are currently released on bail under strict conditions pending the investigation Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment the day of the incident, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the "suspicious vehicles" that were reported near the base. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil." He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network. Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas." Tehran has accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident, along with other accusations of coordinating attacks in the UK. RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.

item.title: Saudi Arabia's military struggle against Houthi attacks
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militia continues to escalate its attacks on Saudi Arabia targeting energy facilities but, above all, airports. On Saturday, a missile attack on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and injured more than 300. In a second attack on Sunday, the militia killed another civilian and injured 11 others. According to their own statements, the Houthis also attacked Saudi Arabia's airport in Dammam and two oil facilities within the past 24 hours. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud warned of the consequences for energy security and announced a strong response. According to a report by the US think tank American Enterprise Institute, Saudi Arabia is targeting Houthi missile launch pads, storage facilities and other military infrastructure in Yemen. The institute quotes Saudi military spokesman Turki al-Maliki in its October 11 report as saying that 136 military targets have already been destroyed. However, years of Saudi-led military intervention between 2015 and 2022 in Yemen have not succeeded in defeating the Houthi militia. Moreover, the Saudi-led international coalition formed in 2015 has fallen apart and the United Arab Emirates has withdrawn its troops. The Iran-aligned Houthis not only control large parts of northern Yemen but also increasingly the western coastline from where they disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea and the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait. In early September, drones also severely damaged the Saudi East-West oil pipeline. The temporary shutdown disrupted oil exports and increased risks for the energy markets. Saudi Arabia calls on Pakistan, Turkey, the United States For weeks, the Saudi government has been seeking allies in the fight against the Houthi militia. In late September, the United Kingdom and France pledged military support to defend Saudi infrastructure. London offered aerial refueling for Saudi fighter jets, while Paris announced it would provide troops, radar systems and air defense technology to protect the Yanbu oil terminal. However, while the US recently refused to fight alongside Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, there could now be a change of heart in Washington, writes political analyst Osamah Al-Rawhani in a study by the Yemeni think tank Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies. He notes that it remains to be seen whether this could actually lead to a successful offensive, as holding on to captured territories and launching counterattacks require significant financial resources, political commitment and the necessary resolve. In his view, it is questionable whether Saudi Arabia would be able to muster the necessary perseverance. The kingdom could, however, change its current strategy. "If the costs of the war continue to rise, Riyadh might look for a way to withdraw from the conflict," Al-Rawhani says. Saudi Arabia's asymmetrical war against the Houthis Marcus Schneider, project manager at the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Center of Expertise on Peace and Security in the Middle East and North Africa, shares a similar view. "To eliminate the Houthis, ground troops would be needed but Riyadh has no experience with this type of warfare, especially in a foreign country," Schneider recently told DW. As such, he believes the Saudi leadership is less concerned with achieving a military victory than with reducing its vulnerability, securing the broadest possible coalition of partners and gaining political maneuvering room. "The Houthis are well-entrenched in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows. Above all, Saudi Arabia needs stability for its Vision 2030 reform set and that is currently further away than ever," Schneider said. He added that military asymmetry is also a key factor: Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. The Houthis, on the other hand, do not need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to deploy missiles and drones, threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping traffic. Are the UAE, Pakistan, Turkey changing course? Saudi Arabia may also be able to turn to another partner in the region: the United Arab Emirates (UAE). According to media reports, Anwar Gargash, a senior diplomatic advisor to the UAE president, spoke out in favor of closer security cooperation among the Gulf states. "We are all targets," he stated on X. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have undermined the security of the entire region, he notes. "It is necessary to revitalize cooperation among the Gulf states, particularly in the areas of security and defense, and to strengthen the collective security system," Gargash added. Pakistan, which signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in early August along with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, also initially ruled out military intervention. According to media reports, however, the country is now said to be carrying out airstrikes on Houthi missile and drone positions — a claim that Islamabad denies. Pakistan does not intend to deploy ground troops. Turkey, another member of the Mecca Pact, rules out an offensive military operation but is providing air defense equipment. Saudi Arabia can thus build on additional military support, according to an analysis by the US think tank Soufan Center. Whether this will result in an effective strategy, however, depends on whether the partners go beyond limited airstrikes and political expressions of solidarity and on whether the fragmented Yemeni government forces can better coordinate their military operations. Meanwhile, Iran has offered to act as a mediator between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. However, given Iran's support for the Houthis and the recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, it is questionable whether Saudi Arabia will accept this offer. Saudi Arabia and the US are allies, whereas Iran and the US have been at war since February. It is also unclear whether Tehran wields sufficient influence over the Yemeni militia to persuade it to halt the attacks. This article was originally published in German.
